After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object.
  • Scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission.
  • Industry observers note that the telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object. The instrument, built in the UK, successfully detected X-rays from the Crab Nebula, one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, marking an important milestone for the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's BepiColombo mission.

Scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission. Their initial results are highly encouraging, arriving just as BepiColombo prepares to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21.

Industry observers note that the telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly. Although engineers monitored MIXS throughout the journey, the instrument could not look directly into space until September. That opportunity came after the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the two science orbiters, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) or Mio.

With its view finally unobstructed, MIXS could begin the critical tests needed before the spacecraft enters its planned orbit around the solar system's smallest planet.

A Telescope's First Look Across 6,500 Light-Years.

For its first astronomical target, the team selected the Crab Nebula, located approximately 6,500 light-years from Earth. This well-studied remnant of an exploded star produces a strong, predictable X-ray signal, making it an ideal reference for testing the telescope's performance.

By examining how MIXS observes this distant object, researchers can determine whether the instrument still performs as expected after its lengthy journey. They can also compare the results with laboratory measurements collected in 2015, when the telescope was last tested on Earth.

Sources indicate that the main observation campaign took place on September 11 and 12. Over 39 hours, the spacecraft carried out 55 carefully controlled changes in orientation to collect the data.

Sources indicate that one crucial measurement was the telescope's angular resolution, which describes its ability to distinguish small details in an image. Scientists determined this by examining how widely the Crab Nebula's X-ray signal spread across the detector. Remarkably, MIXS delivered slightly sharper resolution than it had during its laboratory tests in 2015.

That improvement is particularly encouraging because the instrument will eventually use its X-ray vision to investigate the composition of Mercury's surface.

Better Than Expected After Eight Years in Space.

Professor Emma Bunce, Principal Investigator (PI) for MIXS and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester, welcomed the results as a major achievement for the international team responsible for developing the instrument.

Industry observers note that professor Bunce stated: "We have waited a long time to make measurements with MIXS and it is fantastic to see it operating brilliantly in space. This is testament to our engineering and technical team, and our international partners who we have worked with over many years to build this incredible instrument. 80% of the technology on MIXS is new!

Industry observers note that "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out. We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the Sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after 8 years in space.

"We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase.".

In a recent development, the results suggest that the telescope has weathered its long exposure to the harsh space environment exceptionally well. Engineers have found no unwanted visible light interfering with its images, and the effects of high-energy cosmic rays are understood well enough to be removed during data processing.

In a recent development, the team has also identified a small amount of X-ray emission originating within the instrument itself when sunlight strikes its optics. However, this effect is not expected to interfere with observations of Mercury's sunlit surface. Most importantly, the detector shows no signs of radiation damage after eight years in space.

Some remaining effects still require investigation, and scientists expect to make further adjustments after the spacecraft reaches Mercury to ensure that MIXS is ready for its full scientific mission.

How X-Rays Will Reveal Mercury's Hidden Chemistry.

Sources indicate that bepiColombo is designed to investigate Mercury in unprecedented detail. As the smallest and one of the least explored rocky planets in our solar system, Mercury offers scientists a rare opportunity to understand how planets form and change under the extreme conditions found close to a star.

One of the mission's major goals is to uncover the planet's chemical composition and geological history. These findings could help explain Mercury's unusual characteristics while providing broader insights into the formation and evolution of the solar system.

Recent findings suggest that MIXS, carried aboard the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), will play a central role in this investigation. Developed by a European consortium led by the University of Leicester, it draws on the university's long history of X-ray astronomy research.

It is the first imaging X-ray telescope to operate on a planetary science mission. Working alongside other scientific instruments, MIXS will help produce a global map showing the elements that make up Mercury's surface, revealing its atomic composition in greater detail than ever before. It is also the only UK-led scientific instrument aboard BepiColombo and receives support from the UK Space Agency.

Industry observers note that the instrument works by detecting fluorescent X-rays released by rocks on Mercury's surface. When powerful X-rays from the Sun strike these rocks, they can cause atoms within the material to emit X-rays of their own. Different elements produce characteristic X-ray signals, allowing scientists to identify what the surface is made of without collecting physical samples.

MIXS will make these measurements with assistance from the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), which monitors the solar radiation and particles reaching Mercury.

Recent findings suggest that the telescope will also examine X-rays emitted from Mercury's nighttime surface when charged particles associated with the planet's magnetic environment strike it. These measurements could reveal notable connections between Mercury's surface and the surrounding space environment.

A 10 Billion Kilometer Journey With a Personal Legacy.

In a recent development, for Dr. Adrian Martindale, MIXS Instrument Scientist at the University of Leicester's School of Physics and Astronomy, the successful observations represent the culmination of more than two decades of work.

Martindale joined the project in 2003 while still an undergraduate student and has been involved in nearly every aspect of the instrument's development.

According to recent reports, dr. Martindale mentioned: "BepiColombo, and MIXS in particular, are like part of my family. I've been involved since I was an undergraduate and touched almost every part of the instrument before it was debuted.

"This first data is mind-blowing to me. The last time we could see through this telescope it was in the basement under the School of Physics and Astronomy in Leicester, but after a rocket launch, eight years in space and 10 billion kilometers traveled it looks just the same. I can't wait to see the science data it produces when we get into orbit.".

Industry observers note that the milestone also carries special meaning for the team because MIXS represents the scientific legacy of Professor George Fraser. Fraser was the instrument's original Principal Investigator and the driving force behind its innovative optical design before his death in March 2014.

Professor Bunce added: "We are thinking of George as we operate MIXS fully in space for the first time and know that he would be very, very proud of the team and delighted at our first light observations.".

BepiColombo Prepares for Its Final Arrival at Mercury.

BepiColombo began its arrival phase on September 3, when the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the spacecraft assembly.

The remaining connected spacecraft are scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21. The two science orbiters, MPO and Mio, are then expected to separate on December 9 to 10, allowing them to prepare for their respective scientific operations.

The mission's primary science phase is scheduled to begin in April 2027. Once underway, BepiColombo will investigate Mercury's surface, internal structure, magnetic field, and surrounding environment, helping scientists piece together the history of a planet that remains surprisingly mysterious despite its proximity to the Sun.

For the MIXS team, the successful first observations of the Crab Nebula offer an early indication of what the instrument may accomplish when it finally turns its attention to Mercury.

International Collaboration and Funding.

Recent findings suggest that MIXS was developed through a partnership involving research institutions and technology companies across Europe. Participating organizations include:.

UK funding for the BepiColombo MIXS instrument comes from the UK Space Agency, which serves as the lead funding organization, along with STFC, the European Space Agency, and the University of Leicester.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Huw Edwards, the former BBC news anchor who in 2024 was convicted of three counts of making indecent images of children, will speak publicly about his criminal actions and downfall for the first time in a fresh Channel 4 doc.

“Huw Edwards — Guilty,” airing on Dec. 1, is described as a “stark exploration of a disgraced public figure in the aftermath of a shocking fall from grace.” Related Stories Mike Newell Recalls Being Shot at in Colombia While Filming ‘Love in the Time of Cholera’ With Giovanna Mezzogiorno: ‘She Was Like, “F— All This!”’.

Filmed over nearly a year and capturing Edwards at home in rural Wales, the doc follows a man who for years was one of the most respected voices on British TV as he’s forced to confront his loss of fame, declining health, fractured relationships and his crimes.

“From trusted national figure to registered sex offender,” indicates the voiceover in a short trailer for the documentary, in which an agitated Edwards says that he’d “lost the plot” when asked what he thought he was doing.

Edwards served as lead presenter of the “BBC News at 10” from 2003 and 2023 as well as the BBC News’ chief presenter, and would anchor coverage of major events such as the death and state funeral of Queen Elizabeth II and the coronation of Charles III and Camilla. However, this came crashing down in 2024 following allegations of workplace misconduct and a police investigation into child pornography. He would plead guilty to making indecent images of children and be given a six-month suspended sentence.

“Channel 4 has an established reputation for tackling controversial subjects through exemplary filmmaking,” said Sacha Mirzoeff, senior commissioning editor at Channel 4. “‘Huw Edwards – Guilty’ is no exception in its quest for answers from a man who is trying to come to terms with his abuse of power.”.

In a recent development, added director Patrick Forbes: “This was an important film to make. It’s rare to find a subject that touches on so many significant contemporary concerns – whether it’s celebrity culture or the power of the media – as well as enduring questions about crime and punishment.”.

“Huw Edwards – Guilty” was commissioned by Mirzoeff and produced by Oxford Films. It was directed by Forbes. The producer is Stephanie Collins, with Vanessa Tuson and Nick Kent as executive producers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prime Video’s "Blade Runner 2099" has arrived with an 8-episode limited series revealing what the "Blade Runner" world looks like 50 years after the events of director Denis Villeneuve’s "Blade Runner 2049.".

The most obvious change in this depressing dystopia is that replicants are running the LA show after some unmentionable ecological disaster and humans are now the ones relegated to underclass citizens.

Starring Michelle Yeoh as a replicant cop named Olwen whose life clock is running out and Hunter Schafer as Cora, a desperate human posing as a replicant blade runner, "Blade Runner 2099" unties these two in a mystery revolving around a rogue blade runner and a deadly secret that might cause their city to implode.

We connected with three of the sci-fi show’s main co-stars, Matthew Needham ("House of the Dragon"), Lewis Gribben ("T2 Trainspotting") and Dimitri Abold ("Love Addicts") to hear more about working with creator/showrunner Silka Louisa, and immersing themselves in "Blade Runner 2099's" vivid futuristic worldbuilding.

"For me it's a lot simpler than egos because he's such a goal-oriented person and all of his stuff has such a police procedural quality to it," Needham tells SPACE regarding his role as Yahya, an emotionless replicant who despises all humans.

According to recent reports, "It was really fun to just follow what Silka [Louisa] did. She wrote this great, really exciting mystery thriller, and I just got to play in that.”.

Scottish actor Gribben portrays Cora's ailing younger brother Elias, who has compromised mobility and a rocky relationship with his overprotective sister.

"I've played a few characters that were fairly vulnerable or insular," he notes. "Then seeing the journey of this character grow in strength and confidence and feel like becoming his own man was so compelling to me. It’s almost a relationship that falls apart between brother and sister, and that's fascinating to me because that’s such a cool dynamic you don’t always really see in television reveals. That was quite interesting and made me want to try and be in it.".

In a recent development, as Bebeto, a doctor, veteran of the replicants vs. humans war, and a black-market dealer helping his species procure IDs and passports off-world, Abold enjoyed exploring the many facets of his character.

"Much like Matthew and Lewis, for me it was the journey that Bebeto goes on," Abold adds. "Starting out as someone who’s so hopeful and has to try and scrape up the last dregs of hope as things start falling apart. Being subject to circumstances like that inherently make for an interesting story arc and story in general. Throwing myself into that, especially after how well Silka crafted the story and script, was something I was totally ready for.".

"Blade Runner 2099’s" sets and locations feature detailed production design that allowed the actors to experience a seamless transition into the complex shoot.

"For me and Dimitri, our first day was in Bebeto’s apartment, and it was all so well-realized,” Gribben recalls.

It has been revealed that "You saw all the gadgets because obviously Bebeto was a bit of a tinkerer of a character and had lots of machinery and works and stuff. It took up about 70% of the acting, and we just had to come with compelling conviction. It made it so easy. When you audition for these things, you feel like you have to act more because you’re in a blue screen vacuum. But then you’re there, and it’s so visually well created like that, it made it so easy to be immersed in it.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, stated it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the company. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance noted in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance said auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says.

Trading in the firm’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog introduced an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement said. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

— Michelle Toh contributed reporting.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The first season of The Lowdown had a pretty clear resolution: The story that “truthstorian” Lee Raybon (Ethan Hawke) had been chasing throughout the season — about the death of the brother (Tim Blake Nelson) of Oklahoma’s likely next governor (Kyle Maclachlan) and their family’s corrupt history — was printed (if not in the form he initially thought) and seemingly put to rest.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[This story contains spoilers for season two of The Lowdown and “The Tower,” the Nov. 25 season finale.].

The first season of The Lowdown had a pretty clear resolution: The story that “truthstorian” Lee Raybon (Ethan Hawke) had been chasing throughout the season — about the death of the brother (Tim Blake Nelson) of Oklahoma’s likely next governor (Kyle Maclachlan) and their family’s corrupt history — was printed (if not in the form he initially thought) and seemingly put to rest.

Season two, however, concludes with multiple threads still untied — and some even circling back to season one. Related Stories TV 'American Horror Story' Finale: Paul Anthony Kelly on the Season 13 Ending: "I Was Flabbergasted" TV 'Snowfall' Spinoff Boss Malcolm Spellman Lays Out Multi-Season Proposal for 'The Drop,' Why Season One Was Just a "Dash of What's Coming".

Lee, with help from some of the journalists he disparaged at the beginning of the season, gets an exposé on conditions at Judge Sallsman’s (John Hawkes) Fresh Start meatpacking operations published, but he’s frustrated that he can’t tie the judge himself to the story. As he continues chasing leads — including getting Martha Plimpton’s Sheriff Thorne to go on record about the judge — Marty (Keith David) saves Lee from walking into a confrontation with some of the people behind last season’s One Well conspiracy. They realize that Lee’s story about Fresh Start, the One Well people and Marty’s investigation of the illicit sale of indigenous artifacts are all part of a bigger picture. Ginger (Betty Gilpin), meanwhile, leaves Tulsa after realizing that, for several reasons, she can’t continue her life there.

In other words, there is a lot left to explore in a potential third season — which FX hasn’t decided on yet.

According to recent reports, “I’m trying to twist their arm,” The Lowdown creator and showrunner Sterlin Harjo told The Hollywood Reporter about the very open-ended finale. “We left it open and pushed forward to a season three because I like three-season shows. I don’t know if we’re going to be doing it, but I hope that we are.”.

The finale, titled “The Tower,” did offer closure on one front: Lee, his daughter Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong) and their family and friends lay Tommy Lee Jones’ Lee Sr., aka Frog, to rest at a somewhat chaotic funeral, which features the return of Peter Dinklage as Lee’s friend Wendell, who eulogizes Frog with a reading of Dylan Thomas’ “Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night.” That’s followed by a more relaxed, and touching, gathering at Sweet Emily’s afterward, where Francis reads a journal entry of Frog’s detailing the apprehension he felt about being a father when Lee was a baby.

In a recent development, “He’s going through the stages of grief. How he understands and reinterprets he and his father’s relationship now that his father’s gone, it’s going to be an ever-changing thing,” Hawke tells THR. “But I feel like something positive and profound happens to Lee when his daughter is reading to him.”.

Harjo and Hawke talked with THR about the loose plot threads, Lee’s ongoing work of becoming a better person, and how a conversation between Harjo and Jones led to the finale’s prologue. (Separate interviews are combined and edited below.).

Sources indicate that before we talk about the end of the season, I want to go back to episode six — where Frog dies at the end of a father-son road trip — because the scenes with Ethan and Tommy are just so, so good. It seems like a huge theme of the season of Lee coming to terms with his dad. He’s kind of starting to get there throughout that episode, but there’s still a lot left for him to process.

In a recent development, STERLIN HARJO I would say so. You have this like these two guys that don’t communicate well. I kind of like compare it to the Tim and Dawn love story in the English Office. They have to hide all of their affection, so a touch on the shoulder becomes like a kiss. It’s similar with Lee and Frog because they don’t communicate. These small gestures end up feeling really big. I think them connecting and going home, they don’t say ‘I love you’ or anything like that. But he touches his son on the back. He tells some stories about [Lee’s] mother. All of these things are really big, because they don’t communicate that well, and they have a hard time meeting each other in the middle.

Industry observers note that I think that that last scene is beautiful where Frog claims to Lee, you know, and it almost escapes out of his mouth, “It wasn’t so bad in there, the hospital, and I might have needed a rest.” That’s the apology. Lee is kind of shocked and can’t say anything, and he just nods, which is also his apology and acknowledgement of it. It’s really beautiful moment. And those are my kids that are playing with the bubbles [as Frog watches Lee walk into the convenience store]. I’m really proud of all that.

ETHAN HAWKE What I like about the writing of the show is it’s never one thing. It’s like more like real life. There is the possibility of healing. It kind of dawns on him at the end of episode six that his father wants to make up with him. And if his father wants to do that, then his father is a different man than he had assumed he was. That opportunity for healing existing is a great benefit to Lee. But of course, they don’t really get to resolve it, and that’s the beauty of episode eight when his daughter is reading from [Frog’s] journal to him.

Would the Lee of season one have been able to hand off the Fresh Start story?

HAWKE No. Those are the small growths that you get to show in a TV show. What I love about it, having never made a TV show before, the canvas size is just so big that you can really get intimate with a character and show those little adjustments. I don’t think at the beginning of season one that he would have been able to go to his ex-wife’s wedding and not make it about himself. That was a small journey. This journey of showing respect to other journalists was [another].

HARJO It’s such a substantial deal for me. I wanted that to be a big moment. I opened the season with him calling everyone sellouts and assholes, and then he has to humble himself and go to all of them, hat in hand, and say I need your help. I think it’s also a part of the growth of his personal life and the relationship with his father — him having to realize that he’s not the only one. The story isn’t just about him.

There are a lot more loose ends at the end of this season than there were at the end of season one.

Recent findings suggest that HARJO We’ve got to twist FX and Disney’s arm for season three. I don’t know how the powers that be work that out. It sure would help if we had awards. Somehow, the Hollywood awards have always been elusive to me and my projects, even though they get reviewed so well. We’ll see what happens, but hopefully something like that happens and that helps us a little bit. I don’t know where we stand right now. I hope to do a season three.

Assuming you do go get to go forward — I hope so too — would those loose ends be the primary plot driver in a third season, or more secondary?

Sources indicate that HARJO It will be the plot of season three, that bigger conspiracy. Obviously there will be some surprises, but what I wanted to do was the idea that season one, you feel like it’s one and done. This is the conspiracy. Then we’re moving on to another conspiracy in season two. One of the things I keep saying in season one is everything’s connected. And actually in Reservation Dogs, we stated that a lot too. But the idea is that we were kind of pretending it was going to be these two separate things, but actually they’re all connected.

HAWKE The setup is pretty clear. At the end of season two, we see that there’s a connection between the crime of season one and the crime of season two. There’s a connection between this judge and One Well. I think season three would be about bringing the whole tower down.

From a character perspective, what do you want to keep exploring with Lee?

HAWKE We’ve always kind of dreamed of this as a trilogy. Put simply, season one is about him learning how to be a father, and season two is learning about how to be a son, and a third season would be about him learning to live with himself, and completing the hero’s journey.

HARJO I’m really interested in season three being about, What is it like watching your daughter become the next stage of all of that? And also, what does it mean to slow down? What does it mean to look at your life and go, OK, I don’t always have to chase the truth at the detriment of my health, I can also have balance. How do I balance my life, find happiness and find love, and I’m able to be a father and a son and also someone that fights for the truth. How do we become a whole human being and be more responsible? I think that is in the cards for Lee.

There weren’t any obvious markers for where Ginger has ended up in her final scene. Where is she as she tries to get away from her former life?

Sources indicate that HARJO She’s in Eureka Springs [Arkansas], which is a couple hours away from Tulsa going east, and it’s just an interesting old mining and brothel town. It’s really beautiful, in the Ozarks, and a great place to go to get away. We broke off with Betty and took a small group to Eureka Springs and filmed that.

I also wanted to ask about the prologue scene in the finale, showing Frog at the fireworks stand in Texas and watching Paris, Texas, which the opening scene of the season pays homage to. Did you just want to give people a sense of where he started this season?

Sources indicate that HARJO Tommy Lee Jones would call me up now and again. “Hey, I want to talk about the script. You want to come over?” I’d go to his house, and his wife Dawn was awesome, and we would talk about polo or whatever for a little bit. Then he’d say, “All right, come back here,” and we’d go into his office and start talking about the script. At one point, he goes, “Would you like to know where Frog came from?” And I was like, “What do you mean?” He’s like, “Well, the backstory that I came up with.” I was like, “Yeah, of course.” He just told me that story, and I was amazed. It was just the backstory that he had invented — Frog was in Palestine, Texas, working at this fireworks stand. He told me this story, and I was like, “Well, I’ve got to do that. I have to put that in the finale.” So we did.

Industry observers note that thanksgiving is almost here, and for some folks, the most key part of the holiday isn't the food, family, or football. It's watching a bunch of substantial floats during a parade in Latest York City.

OK, maybe that's not literally true, but the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is an annual touchstone for lots of folks, and it's almost here. As always, there are lots of things to know about it, such as when it starts, where you can watch it, and, this year especially, whether the weather will affect the parade as expected. Let's get into it.

First and foremost, the parade starts at 8:30 a.m. ET and runs until noon on Saturday. Yes, you read that right: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is not actually on Thanksgiving Day this year. There are very good reasons for that, which we'll get to in a second.

According to recent reports, it's worth noting that, unlike most other live televised events, it will not air simultaneously in every time zone. Instead, per NBC News, it will air from 8:30 to around noon in each time zone, so no matter where you are, turn the TV on at 8:30.

The parade will air on NBC, so if you have a TV that gets local channels via cable, an antenna, or another way to watch TV, just turn on NBC.

If you don't have any of those things, Peacock will work, too. I should note that you'll need at least Peacock Premium to stream your local NBC station, and there is no free trial for that. You'll either have to pay $12.99 per month or borrow someone else's login. According to NBC News, this year's parade will feature 100 inflatables in total, the most they've ever used for one of these. You can see the full balloon lineup on the Macy's website, but rest assured that all your favorites are likely included, like Sonic the Hedgehog and the Pink Panther. There are also newly introduced ones, like a DoorDash float and a GEICO float. One float will also act as a tribute of sorts for Fiona the hippo, which is nice.

It has been revealed that performers include Teddy Swims and Megan Moroney on the main stage, with other floats featuring acts such as the Baha Men, Blues Traveler, Icona Pop, and Devo. There's a little something for everyone.

And now for the bad news: There's a weather system moving up the East Coast that has caused the parade organizers to reschedule it this year, per NBC News.

Two storms combined into one in the American South, with the result expected to bring wind gusts of up to 45mph to Upcoming York City starting on Thursday morning. This is a problem because the city has an upper limit of 34mph for gusts regarding substantial inflatable objects. The parade was still scheduled for Thursday until the middle of Wednesday afternoon, when organizers and New York City officials decided to push it back to Saturday.

Unfortunately, that means you'll need a strategy B for Thursday morning entertainment, but, more importantly, this should keep everyone who planned to attend the parade on Thursday safe.

#196577. NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1650 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.
  • It has been revealed that the historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m.
  • The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. After more than 49 years of traveling through space, humanity's most distant spacecraft is now approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from home. At that distance, even a signal moving at the speed of light needs an entire day to make the journey.

It has been revealed that the historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST). Scientists and engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, received a signal from Voyager 1 early Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone.

The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.

Voyager 1 Is Now 24 Light-Hours From Earth.

Astronomers often describe enormous cosmic distances in terms of how long light takes to travel them. A light-day represents the distance light covers in 24 hours, or roughly 16.1 billion miles.

Sources indicate that light moves through a vacuum at approximately 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) per second. To put Voyager 1's distance in perspective, sunlight passing Earth takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon. Reaching Neptune takes roughly four hours, while traveling from Neptune to Voyager 1 requires another 20 hours.

Even these enormous distances are small compared with those separating stars. A single light-year, the distance light travels in one year, measures approximately 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1's extraordinary distance also creates a major challenge for mission controllers. Sending a command to the spacecraft now requires 24 hours, and receiving a response takes another 24 hours. A complete exchange therefore spans two full days, even though the signals travel at the fastest speed possible.

Sources indicate that the milestone comes as engineers investigate a communication problem. NASA has not received scientific or engineering data from Voyager 1 since November 14. However, the probe continues transmitting a carrier signal, the radio signal that normally carries information back to Earth. By tracking this signal and calculating the spacecraft's trajectory, mission specialists were able to verify that Voyager 1 had crossed the one light-day mark. Engineers are continuing to investigate why the expected data is not coming through.

A Historic Journey Beyond the Solar System's Planets.

Industry observers note that voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, were released in 1977 to take advantage of an unusual arrangement of the outer planets. The alignment allowed the spacecraft to use planetary gravity to travel from one destination to another, making an ambitious exploration mission possible.

Sources indicate that managed by JPL, the Voyagers became the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn. They also delivered the first high-resolution images of these distant planets, revealing extraordinary new details about their atmospheres, rings, and moons. Voyager 2 continued farther, becoming the first spacecraft to explore Uranus and Neptune up close.

Sources indicate that today, both probes are traveling through interstellar space, making them humanity's only spacecraft to have crossed into the region beyond the Sun's protective bubble. Their instruments continue monitoring changes in the Sun's magnetic field across immense distances, providing scientists with measurements that cannot be collected from Earth.

Sources indicate that "Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets," remarked Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "But it went on to become central to NASA's fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.".

"Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery," said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. "Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward latest frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.".

Voyager's Golden Record Carries a Message From Earth.

The Voyager spacecraft carry more than scientific instruments. Each also holds a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing images and sounds representing life on Earth. These recordings were designed as messages that an advanced extraterrestrial civilization might discover someday.

The records give the mission a purpose extending far beyond its scientific discoveries. Even after the spacecraft eventually lose the ability to communicate with Earth, they will continue traveling through space with a small collection of sights and sounds from the planet that rolled out them.

"Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward," noted Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. "Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.".

Exploring the Mysterious Region Beyond the Sun.

Voyager 1 is at the moment moving through space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to cross the boundary of the heliosphere, a vast region surrounding the Sun that is filled with particles and magnetic fields generated by our star.

According to recent reports, this protective bubble helps shield the solar system from cosmic radiation arriving from elsewhere in the galaxy. Beyond its outer boundary lies interstellar space, where particles and magnetic fields from the broader galaxy become more dominant.

Industry observers note that voyager 2 followed a different route and crossed into interstellar space in 2018. Together, the probes are providing the first direct observations of conditions beyond the heliosphere.

In a recent development, one of their most intriguing discoveries is that the Sun's effects do not simply disappear at the boundary. Its influence appears to extend much farther into interstellar space than scientists once understood, raising new questions about where the environment shaped by our star truly gives way to the surrounding galaxy.

Industry observers note that "The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere," said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. "One substantial surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.".

How NASA Is Keeping Voyager 1 Alive After Nearly 50 Years.

Operating spacecraft built nearly half a century ago requires increasingly inventive engineering. Both Voyagers have experienced problems as their equipment ages, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer. NASA engineers have repeatedly developed solutions that allow the probes to continue working despite these setbacks.

Sources indicate that electricity has become one of the mission's greatest limitations. Earlier in 2026, engineers took a calculated risk by switching off three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replacing them with three alternatives that consume less power. This change was intended to help the spacecraft stretch its remaining energy supply.

Voyager 1 depends on a radioisotope thermal generator that is now approximately 50 years old. Often described as a nuclear battery, the device produces electricity by converting heat released during the radioactive decay of plutonium.

Sources indicate that as the radioactive material continues to decay, the available power gradually decreases. Both Voyager spacecraft lose approximately four watts of electrical output every year, forcing engineers to make difficult decisions about which systems can remain operational.

The latest conservation measures are expected to provide enough power to operate the spacecraft's current scientific instruments until at least the summer of 2027, when both probes will celebrate their 50th launch anniversaries.

One Day, Voyager 1 Will Become a Silent Messenger to the Stars.

Maintaining contact across such staggering distances requires some of NASA's most powerful communications equipment. The agency relies on its Deep Space Network, a worldwide system of large radio antennas located at three facilities, to communicate with Voyager and other spacecraft traveling to and beyond the Moon.

In a recent development, despite the enormous communication delay and the spacecraft's aging systems, engineers continue monitoring Voyager 1 daily and transmitting instructions every week. The mission remains an extraordinary demonstration of what long-term spacecraft engineering can achieve.

Industry observers note that "We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to," said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. "Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity's silent ambassador to the stars.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that nitesh Tiwari’s “Ramayana” has doubled visitor numbers at Kerala’s Jatayu Earth’s Center, known locally as Jatayu Rock, Ministry of Tourism joint secretary Harikishore S. told a WAVES Film Bazaar panel in Goa, where Indian officials pitched a single-window filming portal and state incentives to international producers. The site is traditionally held to be where the mythical bird Jatayu fell after battling Ravana, a fight the film depicts.

In a recent development, producers on the same stage stated crew skill and speed give India an edge, though Sunita Ram of Rasika Pictures warned the country still lacks the studio space to keep its biggest shoots at home. Related Stories Mike Newell Recalls Being Shot at in Colombia While Filming ‘Love in the Time of Cholera’ With Giovanna Mezzogiorno: ‘She Was Like, “F— All This!”’.

The session, “Filming in India: India’s Rise as a Global Production Hub,” featured Prithul Kumar, joint secretary, broadcasting, at the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting; Harikishore; Alan McAlex, founder of Suitable Pictures (“Santosh,” “Sister Midnight”); and Ram, whose Rasika Pictures handles service production and co-productions (“A Suitable Boy,” “120 Bahadur”).

Kumar said the India Cine Hub portal first went live at Film Bazaar on Nov. 21, 2015. At the time, it mainly handled film visas and permissions for foreign productions. In 2023, the ministry widened its scope after concluding that overseas producers also needed support on the ground and a way to find local resources. The portal now combines permission applications with directories of crew, equipment and services, an interactive location map, and information on state and central incentives.

Industry observers note that state governments, local administrations and central agencies including the Railways, the Archaeological Survey of India and the civil aviation authorities, which clear drone use, all sit behind the single window. Each state has a nodal officer who follows up on permissions in person, Kumar said.

“It’s a hundred times more difficult than manufacturing or assembling a product because every step is a new one, and the filmmakers actually have to turn dreams into reality,” Kumar mentioned of filmmaking.

In a recent development, he clarified that the portal is a permissions tool rather than a networking one; collaboration between filmmakers and service providers happens on the separate WAVES Bazaar market platform. Kumar also mentioned the Ministry of Tourism has signed a non-binding, non-commercial MoU with production houses including Netflix, Amazon and JioCinema to encourage more content about India, such as its food, rivers and forests, and to encourage them to shoot in a wider range of places.

Kumar also asked filmmakers in the room to list themselves on India Cine Hub so producers anywhere in the world can find them.

According to recent reports, harikishore stated roughly 80% of what a producer needs comes from the states, with the central ministry handling the other 20%. He pointed to Madhya Pradesh, which he said pays back up to 75% of the cost of a film shot in the state. “And it is not a policy paper; they have given it to 50 people in the last two years,” Harikishore said.

He said the jump in visitors at the site is set to last. In his view, what holds other locations back is a knowledge gap among state decision-makers about what productions actually want, and he proposed workshops in which producers brief officials. Kumar agreed, noting that states tend to upload only tourist landscapes to the portal. “Shooting happens in a village, it happens in a house,” Kumar said. The ministry has also asked states to pick 10 locations from past hit films and brand them, he added, citing Bekal Fort, where a song from “Bombay” was shot. Kumar said Jatayu Rock should likewise carry “Ramayana” branding.

McAlex mentioned India used to draw productions mainly when scripts had Indian stories or characters. “We had projects coming in to shoot American interiors because the actors had a very short window, so they didn’t have to go back to the U.S.,” McAlex said. He added that AI and volume stages are now opening the door to exterior work too, and that local crews and VFX facilities let productions keep everything in one place.

According to recent reports, as examples of Indian crews pulling off complex work, he cited a British Film Institute-funded project whose executives doubted a mid-day firm move in Mumbai could be done. His team managed it. He also pointed to an American production on which only the director and DP flew in, and an all-Indian crew pulled off a stunt sequence on a fifth floor.

In a recent development, ram mentioned international producers are now confident that Indian working standards match those of the U.K., Europe and the U.S., and that they no longer need to fly in large teams when they can mix in local crew. “Every day of shoot is like, you know, launching a rocket every day. But that’s world over, not just India,” Ram said. She tells anyone who doubts what’s possible in India that 24 hours there can equal three weeks of work elsewhere, because “we can turn things around here faster than anywhere else.”.

Ram added that she looks for upcoming locations with every script. One recent project set in Mumbai ended up shooting in the small town of Karaikudi instead. “They’d never even heard of it, but it’s something you introduce, you know, with every film,” she remarked.

WAVES Film Bazaar is the market component of the International Film Festival of India.

CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the company has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices.

"The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner mentioned in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can.".

Walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey remarked Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.

Walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth.

Here's how the firm performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

For the quarter ended Oct. 31, the company reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%.

Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share.

Sources indicate that walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.

Sources indicate that furner also remarked Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

"It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he stated.

Though the company reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more.".

The tech giant on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

The Iowa Lead Detonation Happened. Now the Real Work Begins to Study It

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Wednesday morning, the US Army detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide outside of Middletown, Iowa.
  • Environmental Protection Administration chief Lee Zeldin told CNN shortly after the explosion that preliminary monitoring from the site detected no lead in the air around the site.
  • But the full extent of the fallout may not be certain for at least a few days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Wednesday morning, the US Army detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide outside of Middletown, Iowa.

Environmental Protection Administration chief Lee Zeldin told CNN shortly after the explosion that preliminary monitoring from the site detected no lead in the air around the site.

But the full extent of the fallout may not be certain for at least a few days. A barrage of government, university, and citizen monitoring and testing projects are underway. Air, soil, and water samples they’ve collected will determine the extent of lead exposure, if any, in Middletown and the surrounding area.

The lead azide has been on the base near Middletown for decades, but recently the Army deemed it unstable and too dangerous to move and remediate. Poor communication between the Army and towns in the path of the fallout led to a public uproar. While the federal government stepped up its mitigation measures—the Army dug a dam around the detonation site, while NASA stepped in with research jets and satellites for monitoring—universities had already been swinging into action due to the chaotic rollout.

According to recent reports, several departments at the University of Iowa kicked into gear to begin to set up air and soil monitoring stations late last week. “Initially we did not know that [the] EPA or Army or anybody else was going to be doing anything,” says Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the university.

Scientists at Purdue University, nearly 300 miles away, also put out a call for soil samples from Middletown.

“We learned about the detonation late last week; once we learned of the initial delay in detonation date we decided to put forth the call,” notes Ellen Wells, a professor of public health at Purdue who is helping lead the testing.

Surrounding towns were notified in late October that the Army wanted to conduct pre- and post-detonation soil sampling for “an intentional, controlled detonation” of a “quantity of lead azide”—seemingly the only notification that many towns in the initial modeled path of the fallout say they received before a press release issued by the Army days before the planned explosion.

The lack of communication has, understandably, instilled a lot of public distrust in the federal government, including agencies’ monitoring programs. Thorne says that efforts like the University of Iowa’s are not meant to displace federal monitoring, but rather to supplement and support it—and hopefully reassure the public.

Sources indicate that “We and the EPA are doing similar exposure assessment efforts. If they agree, they can give us some confidence,” he says. “For people who might be concerned about the veracity of what the government tells them, if their findings are in alignment with ours, then I think that helps quell some of those concerns.”.

Industry observers note that thorne says that the soil samples the University of Iowa scientists had measured before the detonation had low levels of lead. “If I saw something like a 10 fold increase in the amount of lead in the soil 20 miles downwind, I’d be concerned with that,” he says.

It has been revealed that some soil testing can be done instantaneously with devices that can image the soil’s surface, using a gun device that fires X-ray beams into a sample and measures the specific electromagnetic signature of lead atoms that bounce back. While Wells and her team don’t have those instruments in the field, they are planning on using them to analyze the samples they receive. More sensitive lab equipment can provide even more granular data, though Thorne estimates those results could take about a week.

In addition to monitoring being done by the Army and the EPA, which is maintaining a live website of air quality results, University of Iowa scientists are monitoring the plume to figure out where the highest concentration of lead may settle. They’re also collecting data on particulate matter in the air around the detonation site for analysis, sending air filters to the lab for more detailed results.

“As these data are compiled over the holiday week to the early next week, I think we'll start to have a bigger picture of roughly how much loading we have of the soil at various places downwind and what we can expect from that,” states Thorne.

According to recent reports, A lot of concern online has centered around how additional lead in the soil may impact crops in Iowa, one of the central agricultural hubs for soybeans and corn. Jeffrey Catalano, a professor of earth and environmental sciences at Washington University in Saint Louis, says that there’s a large amount of research showing that plants like corn are actually pretty bad at absorbing lead.

Sources indicate that “The hazard is more like, if soil with lead in it gets stuck to leaves, and you eat leaves that have lead-rich soil on them,” he notes. “If you take some corn crops next year versus this year and measure their lead content, I don’t think you would see anything other than random variations. I’m not worried about food produced in Iowa.”.

Sources indicate that municipal drinking water is also unlikely to be affected because most treatment plants are designed to remove lead from water supplies, states Patrick McNamara, a professor of environmental engineering at Marquette University. It’s more worrisome for private wells or streams on people’s property where livestock may drink. McNamara suggests that owners use at-home lead water tests for safety.

While the detonation and haphazard announcements leading up to it raised alarm bells, both Thorne and Catalano say that there are communities dealing with legacy pollution around the country that are exposed to dangerous levels of lead every day that deserve attention—and remediation.

In a recent development, “I've done work in places like East Chicago, Indiana, where they built a housing project and a school on the grounds of a former lead smelting plant—we were seeing soil lead levels that are roughly 10,000-fold higher than what we've measured in Iowa this week,” Thorne says. “There are a lot of places around the country where there's a much greater lead hazard than I'm going to anticipate what we’ll end up with here. I don't want to over-sell this one when we recognize that there are places where people are really suffering, and need to be remediated for the health of their children.”.

Latest Update: How Hinges deep-learning Most Compatible feature actually works, and how to train it

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ever since its introduction in 2018, Hinge's "Most Compatible" feature has earned equal parts praise and scorn from online daters, who can't seem to decide if it's the best thing ever or a bad joke.
  • Even today, eight years after it was first introduced, Most Compatible is a marvel of mathematical engineering, beginning with its foundation: the Gale-Shapley algorithm (also known as the propose-and-reject algorithm), developed all the way back in 1962 to solve a (hypothetical) mating problem.
  • Hinge's variation of the algorithm works dynamically, constantly taking into account user preferences and choices to predict what kind of person you would most like to date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ever since its introduction in 2018, Hinge's "Most Compatible" feature has earned equal parts praise and scorn from online daters, who can't seem to decide if it's the best thing ever or a bad joke.

Even today, eight years after it was first introduced, Most Compatible is a marvel of mathematical engineering, beginning with its foundation: the Gale-Shapley algorithm (also known as the propose-and-reject algorithm), developed all the way back in 1962 to solve a (hypothetical) mating problem.

Hinge's variation of the algorithm works dynamically, constantly taking into account user preferences and choices to predict what kind of person you would most like to date. At the start of each latest day, you will receive a Most Compatible profile suggestion that expires after 24 hours unless you interact with it.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections.

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups.

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups.

Pure — best for anonymous hookups.

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

Recent findings suggest that but there's a massive catch here that too many Hinge customers are unaware of: your own actions and inactions are factored into the equation, so if you feed the algorithm bad data, it won't work in your favor, and you'll rarely see a compelling profile suggestion. We reached out to Hinge to gain a better understanding of their algorithm from the inside, and they described it as a "recommendation system" that combines multiple algorithms, "using your stated preferences and your activity on the app," to adjust and refine its suggestions.

Here are three key tips from Hinge to help its recommendation algorithm work for you:.

Too many Hinge owners (and men in particular!) cast a wide net, interacting with as many profiles as possible, sending out Likes all over the place. We get it: the more-is-more approach has its appeal, but it actually hurts the algorithm's effectiveness, since it becomes harder to narrow down your preferences when you're too indiscriminate about who you like or interact with.

Or, as Hinge told us: "If you send too many likes, we can’t tell what you truly want. At the same time, if you rarely send likes, we don’t have enough information to learn from about who excites you. By engaging with others with curiosity and purpose, your recommendations meaningfully evolve alongside you.".

According to recent reports, instead of being overly enthusiastic in your search, be intentional: take your time to vet profiles and interact only with people you can genuinely see yourself dating. You may not even necessarily know what these profiles might have in common, but rest assured the algorithm will be at work in the background finding the common thread and refining its suggestions for you in the future.

According to recent reports, the default Hinge filters are very relaxed, but there's actually a Dealbreakers toggle hidden in the Dating Preferences section of your profile. The normal preferences (location and age range, for example) are taken into account but treated more like guidelines than hard limits. However, if you start enabling your Dealbreakers, Hinge will treat them as hard limits and never even show you profiles that don't match your preferences. As Hinge put it to us, "Hinge will only show you each other if you both meet the dealbreakers that either of you set, such as wanting kids. This helps you focus on people who feel like a real long-term match.".

Most dating app customers, out of sheer eagerness to start browsing local singles, make a half-hearted attempt to fill out their profiles, usually doing the bare minimum to meet the app's requirements. But Hinge offers an extremely generous array of profile fields, and the more you fill out, the more data the algorithm can use to do its matchmaking work.

And as Hinge pointed out to us, not answering a question is treated like a negative, actively shrinking your dating pool: "When you select 'prefer not to say,' it limits who can see you. From family prepares and dating intentions to drinking habits, you're excluded from being shown to people who've set Dealbreakers around those compatibility factors.".

We recommend you put particular focus on filling out Hinge's prompts in a thoughtful way, taking particular care to choose ones that reflect directly on your personality or interests.

Sources indicate that in Hinge's own profile guide, they offer key advice that is too often overlooked: ditch the clichés and one-word or low-effort responses, and take the time to give a personal answer to every question. And take the time to answer a voice prompt, as you'll be rewarded by the algorithm for doing so.

Finally, there's good evidence that Hinge's algorithm rewards profiles with refreshed photos, so if you haven't updated your main photos in a minute, follow their photo refresh guide to optimize your new pics.

If you follow the steps above, you should start to see the algorithm working more in your favor, and you'll look forward to each day's fresh Most Compatible suggestion.

German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, German auto bosses and labor representatives touted their ability to work through their disagreements in a uniquely cooperative process.
  • A series of crises across the industry and abrupt moves by management to slash costs are testing the limits of the German power-sharing agreement.
  • As negotiations between union representatives and Germany's largest carmaker, Volkswagen, began on Tuesday, the balance of power appeared increasingly one-sided.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, German auto bosses and labor representatives touted their ability to work through their disagreements in a uniquely cooperative process. Those days appear to be gone.

A series of crises across the industry and abrupt moves by management to slash costs are testing the limits of the German power-sharing agreement.

As negotiations between union representatives and Germany's largest carmaker, Volkswagen, began on Tuesday, the balance of power appeared increasingly one-sided.

Volkswagen wants to freeze wages for the next two years while cutting several allowances and bonuses.

Alongside Mercedes, it's demanding longer hours under the same pay, with both companies threatening to withhold investment from German factories.

Industry observers note that unions have responded with warning strikes and the threat of larger walkouts. Yet workers are aware of the grim outlook, with Germany's auto industry losing more than 123,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute.

"I think that the labor representatives are in a very difficult situation," said Thomas Haipeter, a labor researcher at the University of Duisburg-Essen. "On the one hand, they have to make concessions in order to safeguard jobs. And despite these massive employment reductions to safeguard the rest of the jobs and locations, what is missing for them is a kind of more offensive strategy.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Labor's outsized role in German auto companies goes back decades and includes a 1945 deal at Volkswagen promising a hot shower a day.

That year marks the start of "co-determination" at the organization, in which workers are represented internally by employee-led workers' councils, as well as by outside labor unions.

Berlin then anchored labor's strong say in Volkswagen in 1960, before the firm issued public shares, ensuring government officials retained extra votes in the supervisory board. Those seats, belonging to the Lower Saxony government, tend to be sympathetic to workers.

Workers' councils, meanwhile, became a fixture across the German auto industry, with representation extending across multiple production sites within the same companies.

Pay and benefits for auto workers have risen over the years. During the last German industry boom, between 2011 and 2019, pay for auto workers clearly outpaced the average German wage.

In early 2025, auto workers were earning nearly a third more per hour than the typical German worker, when bonuses and allowances are factored in, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).

That same year, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume praised cooperation with the unions as one of the organization's "great strengths" during the 80th anniversary of the 1945 agreement.

Cracks were long in the making, according to case studies by Haipeter and others. Labor was increasingly forced to protect plants and jobs as companies chased cheaper workers abroad.

According to recent reports, workers' councils turned their attention to saving their own production lines. They focused on business strategy and even hired business consultants in an effort to sway strategy.

Sources indicate that when combustion engines dominated, autoworkers could argue German production was the most technologically advanced, according to Haipeter. That changed with the shift to electric vehicles.

Sources indicate that "This line of compromise is canceled now by management," he noted. "They say it doesn't matter for us where we produce. We have to produce at the locations or in countries which are best-cost countries and not in countries which have higher wages.".

Slow sales of electric autos and competition from Chinese manufacturers have, meanwhile, exposed the cost difference.

In 2024, Volkswagen abruptly canceled a series of labor agreements and threatened factory closures. After tough negotiations, labor agreed to significant cuts — €1.5 billion yearly in abandoned wage hikes and the elimination of 50,000 positions through attrition — in exchange for job security for current employees through 2030.

It has been revealed that management returned this summer with a restructuring proposal that included the closures of four German plants. It delayed that decision following negotiations, but slated another 50,000 positions for attrition.

Volkswagen declined to comment for this article.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The most sensitive issue for unions may be the demand that employees work more for the same amount of pay, or even receive less for less work.

Industry observers note that the union IG Metall won the concession for a 35-hour workweek in 1984 after seven weeks of strikes. It's now standard in every labor contract in the auto industry, although it's not uncommon for worksites to deviate from the employee agreement, according to Haipeter.

Mercedes has called for employees to agree to an exception across the manufacturer. The company acknowledged that the 35-hour workweek was "hard-won" and "means a great deal" to its workers. "However, the conditions under which it was agreed upon no longer exist today," it said in a statement to DW.

Volkswagen, meanwhile, is demanding greater "flexibility" as the negotiations get underway.

According to recent reports, "They call it flexibility in both directions," Thorsten Gröger, head of negotiations for the union, said last week. "In the end, Volkswagen wants its employees to perform unpaid work.".

The 35-hour workweek is too sacred for unions to give in, remarked Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, a longtime analyst of the German car industry.

"The unions are in a difficult position," he noted. "They battled for a 35-hour workweek, and that's an incredible privilege that comes with a lot of pride. The union knows that as soon as one factory, one production hall, gives up the 35-hour workweek, then they will have a conflagration.".

In a recent development, dudenhöffer sees parallels in another crisis from Volkswagen's history. After a downturn in the early 1990s, the then-head of the German state of Lower Saxony, Gerhard Schröder, pushed for an agreement for workers to work less in exchange for retaining their jobs.

"We need a mediator along these lines," Dudenhöffer said.
