📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Best International Oscar race is the biggest ever — a record 104 international features are in contention, beating the previous high-water mark of 93 set in 2020 — and one of the most open in years.

There is no out-and-out favorite this season, although European cinema again looks strong, with Javier Calvo and Javier Abrosso’s Spanish entry La Bola Negra; Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner Fjord, in the running for Romania; and Pawel Pawlikowski’s Polish contender Fatherland all expected to make the short list, alongside Asian faves including South Korea’s Possible Love, from Lee Chang-dong; and Japan’s All of a Sudden from Ryusuke Hamaguchi.

Sources indicate that behind that top five is a long list of maybes, including French entry Minotaur from twice-nominated Russian director Andrey Zvyagintsev; Lukas Dhont’s WWI drama Coward, Belgium’s entry; Austria’s Rose, which like Fatherland stars Sandra Huller; and Rehearsals for a Revolution, Pegah Ahangarani’s documentary on her family and their battles against the Iranian regime, which is the U.K. official Oscar submission.

It has been revealed that one hundred films were submitted by countries or regions. Four qualified through a new method where movies that win top awards at leading festivals are accepted as long as they meet the language, creative input and theatrical-release requirements for the category. According to Academy rules, an international feature film is defined as a feature-length motion picture (more than 40 minutes) produced outside the United States with a predominantly (more than 50 percent) non-English dialogue track. New Zealand’s submission, Taratoa Stappard’s gothic horror tale Mārama, was dropped for falling short of the language requirement.

Recent findings suggest that academy members from all branches who meet the minimum viewing requirements can participate in the preliminary round of voting for the shortlist, taking place between will take place Dec. 7-11. The shortlist of 15 international films will be confirmed on Dec. 15. Oscar nominations voting will take place Jan. 11-15, 2027, with the nominations announcement on Jan. 21.

The 99th Academy Awards will be held on March 14, 2027.

In a recent development, THR has exhaustively compiled the full list of international contenders, with trailers, reviews and talent interviews where available. Enjoy!

Roland Sejko’s documentary uses archival footage, newsreels and state-produced cinema to examine how Enver Hoxha’s communist regime used film as an instrument of propaganda. Tracing Albania’s isolation and political transformation over four decades, the film explores how the country’s official image was manufactured, controlled and disseminated by the state.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

In 1993, a car crash leaves Ahmed amnesiac, so that not even his family feels familiar. His youngest son fears him and his bandaged face, while Ahmed feels uneasy about his neighbor. Yanis Koussim’s debut feature — the Arabic title means “exorcism” — reimagines the traumas of Algeria’s bloody “Black Decade” (1992–2002), a civil war between the government and Islamist rebel groups, as a horror film, blending memory, trauma and possession.

Teenage angst meets the supernatural in Laura Casabé’s coming-of-age horror film, set over a single lazy summer day in 2001, at the peak of Argentina’s great depression. Amid the backdrop of social unrest, adolescent desire turns deadly in this slow-burn rage thriller, which debuted at Sundance in 2025.

Sources indicate that tamara Stepanyan’s narrative feature debut follows Céline, a French woman who travels to Armenia to settle the affairs of her supposedly deceased husband, Arto. There she discovers that he concealed his past as a soldier and is regarded by some as a deserter. As she investigates his life, Céline encounters a country still haunted by successive wars and their unresolved consequences.

Read THR‘s interview with director Tamara Stepanyan here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Industry observers note that james J. Robinson’s debut feature is the country’s first-ever Tagalog-language submission for the Oscars. The meditative film focuses on an aging woman who questions her faith as the world crumbles around her. After a young construction worker dies under suspicious circumstances, an elderly nun whose life has been shaped by discipline, service and belief, gets drawn into a world of crime and corruption.

The trailer for First Light is below.

According to recent reports, sandra Hüller is everywhere in this season’s awards conversation, but the German star gives her most transformative performance playing a 17th-Century woman passing as a male farmer in Markus Schleinzer’s period drama. Hüller won the Best Performance trophy in Berlin for the role, which was based on hundreds of similar recorded cases throughout history. Read THR’s review of Rose here.

According to recent reports, zaur Gasimli’s historical drama follows Azerbaijani philanthropist Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev and his efforts to establish Baku’s first school for Muslim girls in 1901. Facing fierce opposition from religious conservatives, Taghiyev enlists the support of his young wife, Sona, in a campaign that becomes a test of his influence, diplomacy and determination to expand educational opportunities for women.

In a recent development, mejbaur Rahman Sumon reimagines Adam and Eve in the monsoon-soaked Bengali countryside in this dark folk tale. A tenant farmer (Mostafizur Noor Imran) wants out of his arranged marriage to a woman (Nazifa Tushi) the villagers regard as insane. Promising her a trip to the circus, he rows her into the forest and slips away in the dark. Yet however far he takes her, the thud of a palm fruit beside their hut confirms her return. Sumon’s follow-up to Hawa, Bangladesh’s 2022 Oscar submission, premiered in Rotterdam’s Tiger Competition.

Check out the official trailer below.

Lukas Dhont’s queer World War I drama follows two Belgian soldiers, Pierre and Francis, who find an unexpected refuge from the brutality of the trenches in the world of theatre. Assigned to organize entertainment for their fellow troops, the men develop an increasingly intimate relationship as they put together a revue behind the front lines. Leads Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne shared the Best Actor prize at Cannes.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Recent findings suggest that this Turkish-language political drama from German Academy Award nominee İlker Çatak (The Teacher’s Lounge) qualified for Oscar submission by winning the Golden Bear for Best Film at the Berlinale. Özgü Namal and Tansu Biçer star as Derya and Aziz, a successful theatrical couple whose lives are upended after their latest production brings them into conflict with the authorities in Ankara. Dismissed from their jobs and forced to leave their home, they find their loss of professional standing and financial security puts their marriage under pressure, testing the convictions that once united them.

Read THR‘s interview with Çatak here and THR‘s review of Yellow Letters here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

The coming-of-age drama about tradition, ambition and choosing your own destiny follows a young woman in the Bolivian Andes who takes up the sacred ways of midwifery, but dreams of escaping to the city to become a singer. Directed by Álvaro Olmos Torrico, The Condor Daughter had its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival.

A 60-something electrician has his very ordered life shattered by the sudden death of his wife. Left alone and forced to fend for himself in a strictly patriarchal society, he begins to recognize how much he took her devotion for granted. His attempts to reconnect with his estranged children are further complicated by his discovery that his son is living with another man.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

Allan Deberton’s queer coming-of-age drama, which debuted in Berlin as part of the Generation Kplus section, follows a 12 year-old boy growing up in a small rural community trying balance his affection and desires with the fear of rejection from his father and surrounding community.

Check out a THR interview about the film here and the trailer below.

Nearly a decade after well-received 2017 feature Western, German director Valeska Grisebach returns with another deconstruction of a male-dominated genre. This slow-burning crime thriller, set in the Bulgarian borderlands, works as a low-key arthouse take on The Godfather, as archaeologist Veska (Yana Radeva) returns to the rural community she grew up in and reconnects with old friends, getting pulled back into criminal activity. Winner of the Jury Prize in Cannes.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Recent findings suggest that majid Majidi’s social drama, about Solan (Mohammad Rahimi), a poorly-paid temporary teacher in a remote, drought-stricken Iranian village was the stand out at this year’s Busan Film Festival, where it won the top prize, directly qualifying it for the Oscar race. When the death of the benefactor funding the school’s meal programme threatens to drive away the pupils, Solan takes matters into his own hands, turning to oil smuggling to keep the meals coming.

Check out the trailer for Midday Meal below.

Sources indicate that even the dead face eviction in Polen Ly’s elegiac ghost story about the cost of redevelopment in Cambodia. Thida (Savorn Serak) has watched over a movie house in Battambang since her death during the Khmer Rouge years. With the building marked for demolition, she must choose between wandering as a homeless spirit and risking the pain of another human life. She befriends Hai (Piseth Chhun), a young journalist who remembers going to the movies there as a boy. In the shuttered theater, the two watch a film together on his phone. Ly’s fiction feature debut premiered in Venice’s Biennale College Cinema program and won the Golden Hanoman, the top prize at Indonesia’s Jogja-NETPAC Asian Film Festival.

Sources indicate that nchini Sylvia-Bright is back in her second Cameroon Oscar submission after Ngang Romanus’ 2021 movie Hidden Dreams. In Mabanda, she plays Mojoko, a pregnant teenager who, after the death of her mother, is left alone with her abusive father, played by director Quintus, and faces rejection by her community. Shot in Cameroonian Pidgin English, it’s the eighth submission by the country for the Academy Awards.

Check out the first look trailer below.

This transatlantic drama from Montreal-based director Geneviève Dulude-De Celles bowed in Berlin, where it won the Silver Bear for Best Screenplay. It centers on an art expert, Mihail, who fled Bulgaria 30 years earlier and returns to authenticate the work of Nina, an 8-year-old Bulgarian artist and possible child prodigy, whose paintings have gone viral online. As Mikhail studies her work, he is forced to confront the ghosts of his past.

Check out the trailer for Nina Rosa below.

Industry observers note that the period mystery, the director’s second feature, premiered at Cannes. The follow-up to Martelli’s General Augusto Pinochet-era political thriller Chile ‘76is set in 1992, after Pinochet’s regime ends and a 9-year old girl is staying in an Andean ski resort where she befriends a German teenager aiming to be a competitive skier, only to vanish without a trace.

Read the THR review and an interview with Martelli.

Check out the trailer for The Meltdown below.

Chinese comedy star Shen Teng plays a chef who takes a job in Bahata, a fictional stand-in for Baghdad, to pay off his family’s debts. In this war drama loosely inspired by the 2003 U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, the Chinese restaurant where he works becomes both a refuge for local orphans and a bar for American soldiers. Director Wen Muye previously made a blockbuster out of the high cost of cancer drugs in China with 2018’s Dying to Survive. This latest social drama has grossed $358.4 million worldwide, making it by far the highest-grossing entry in this year’s international feature Oscar race.

A group of misfits converging at Babel, a legendary Colombian dive bar that doubles as purgatory, and where La Flaca — the city’s Grim Reaper — presides. Here, souls gamble years of their lives with her, daring to outwit Death herself. With his feature debut, which debuted at Sundance in 2025, director Gala del Sol has created a fantastical Colombian fever dream where life and death collides and the fate of people is left to chance.

Check out the official trailer below.

Sources indicate that with her debut feature, Costa Rica’s Kim Torres has created a rural chiller, combining story combining a coming-of-age drama with supernatural and thriller elements. The film follows 13-year-old Laura, who feels suffocated by her latest family, despite the lush forests and palm plantations that surround her. She soon discovers the supposed village paradise hides a shadowy secret that preys on the women living in it. Torres’ drama world premiered at San Sebastian’s New Directors sidebar in 2025.

Director Hana Jusic took inspiration from Wuthering Heights and gothic horror in this period drama, set in rural Croatia, circa 1910, to tell a surprisingly modern tale of female liberation. Teresa, a Chilean woman dressed all in black like an avenging angel, arrives in an isolated, and deeply religious community of Croatian shepherds in the early 20th century, claiming to be the widow of a local man who emigrated to South America.

In a recent development, her arrival unsettles the tightly ordered society, challenging its traditional relationships and expectations. Unable to speak the language, she becomes a blank canvas for hopes and fears, particularly of the women in the community.

You can read a director interview here and watch the THR Presents interview with Hana Jusic here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Carlos Larrazabal’s debut feature explores the pull of home and the longing to leave. It follows Elvis, who returns to Havana after spending a decade in prison for murdering his abusive stepfather. As he reconnects with childhood sweetheart and falls back into life in the city’s criminal underworld, Elvis must decide whether to stay in the world he knows or escape Havana for a upcoming life elsewhere.

Cyprus’ first-ever international Oscar contender is also the feature debut of writer-director Myrsini Aristidou. Newcomer Maria Petrova and Christos Passalis, who played the son in Yorgos Lanthimos’ Dogtooth, star as an 11-year-old and her absent, petty criminal father who returns home after a family death. The film won The World Cinema Dramatic Audience Award at Sundance.

Check out the THR’s Presents interview with Myrsini Aristidou here and read an earlier interview with her here.

Prague-based filmmaker Pepa Lubojacki scoured through family photos and diary snapshots for this intimate, heart-rending look at her family’s struggles with alcoholism, addiction and homelessness. The film premiered in Berlin, where it won the best documentary honor as well as the independent Caligari award.

According to recent reports, this historical thriller from directors Yohane Dean Lengol and Hamed Mobasser is set in 1959, in the final months of Belgian colonial rule, in Club Rumba Royale, a popular nightclub where white Europeans and Congolese citizens rub shoulders as dance mixes with debates of independence. Featuring African rumba star Fally Ipupa, the feature is the first submission by DR Congo since 1997 and only the second overall.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

Sources indicate that may el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion-winning Woman Unknown is backdropped by a Danish city free from Nazi occupation, mere months after World War II has ended. It tells the story of Marie (Volpi Cup winner Mathilde Arcel), a young nanny and housemaid about to marry her wealthy, older, and widowed employer, Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund). But Marie guards a shameful secret.

Sources indicate that the Danish filmmaker deftly scrutinizes post-war patriotism and the era’s chastisement of women and their sex lives. “There have been so many films about the Second World War, and that is true,” el-Toukhy told THR ahead of Venice. “But they’re all based mostly on men’s experiences and recollections of war. So that really energized me.”.

Read THR‘s interview with May el-Toukhy here.

Check out a clip from Woman Unknown below.

In a recent development, the second feature film from director Andrés Farías centers on Sonia (Mercedes Morales), a widow who trades her family home for a cramped apartment and finds unexpected intimacy with Aimé, a working-class Haitian man, defying her family and the racial tensions between Dominicans and Haitians. The drama played Havana, Miami and Chicago and won best film, director and actress at the 2026 Dominican Film Festival in New York.

Sources indicate that director Cristina Barragán, who represented Ecuador in 2016 with Alba, continues her exploration of childhood wounds in this drama starring Simone Bucio as Azucena, a woman in her 30s who approaches Julio, a teenager in a group home, played by first-time actor Francis Eddú Llumiquinga. As they spend time together, an uneasy closeness grows, changing the personal bond in ways two outsiders from different worlds, but with a shared experience of trauma, The film won the best screenplay award in the Orizzonti section at the Venice Film Festival.

It has been revealed that the Egyptian-Austrian filmmaker Abu Bakr Shawky is back in the international Oscar race after his 2018 feature Yomeddine, also submitted for Egypt. The Stories, loosely inspired by his own parents’ relationship, follows aspiring Cairo pianist Ahmed and his long-distance romance with Austrian pen pal Liz, from the 1960s through the 1980s. Starring Amir El-Masry (The Crown) and Valerie Pachner (Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore).

Read what the director remarked about The Stories here and then check out the trailer below.

Arturo López Rodas wrote, directed and produced this debut feature, a 60-minute drama in which three old friends reunite for a funeral after decades apart, musing on life, loss and time. It won best screenplay at the Ícaro Awards and best international feature at the Cobb International Film Festival. Vértices represents El Salvador’s first entry into Oscar’s best international feature competition.

Check out the official trailer below.

In a recent development, in his feature film debut, director German Golub charts the real-life story of Erika Salumäe, a track cyclist who overcomes personal and professional hardship — and the pressure of the dwindling Soviet regime — to become a two-time Olympic gold medallist in 1988 and 1992. From troubled young woman to national hero, Salumäe’s tenacity makes this biographical sports drama a story of inspiration and grit, with Estonian actress Karolin Jürise in the titular role.

Check out the trailer for Our Erika below.

Finnish filmmaker Markus Lehmusruusu (2019’s Ricky Rapper and the Strong Man) turns to science fiction in his sophomore feature. In a future, sterile world without nature or animals, Pasi (Miro Lopperi) is a lonely and compassionate designer of synthetic pets.

When by chance he stumbles upon the last surviving squirrel, he decides to defy the very strict regulations of interaction with what little nature is left in the world and help the squirrel back into its natural habitat. Lehmusruusu tackles the intersection of humanity’s instinctive need to both survive and provide in this Fantastic Fest debut (which used real, trained squirrels over animatronics or VFX).

Check out the trailer for The Squirrel below.

It has been revealed that the first feature film from exiled Russian dissident director Andrey Zvyagintsev (Loveless, Leviathan) in nearly a decade is a taut psychological thriller set in Russia shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Loosely inspired by Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife (1969) it follows a wealthy businessman caught between government demands that he recruit employees to send as cannon fodder in the war effort, and his growing suspicions that his wife is having an affair. As pressure mounts on both fronts, his carefully controlled domestic and professional life begins to unravel. Like the Russian state, he goes to extremes of violence to maintain the appearance of power and control.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with director Andrey Zvyagintsev here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

In a recent development, levan Koguashvili’s dramedy is set in a Georgian village struggling to recover from the economic upheaval following the collapse of the Soviet Union. At its center is Zuriko, a widowed hazelnut farmer trying to secure a fair price for his harvest while his debts mount. With the help of his friend Gela, he also embarks on a search for a new partner, despite the objections of his formidable former mother-in-law.

Check out the teaser for the film below.

In a recent development, birgit Minichmayr plays Ella, a mother struggling to process the death of her daughter Jessie, in Sandra Wollner’s drama about grief and the complicated bonds left behind. Ella begins spending time with Lux, Jessie’s boyfriend, who was with her on the night she died. As the two grow closer, their relationship becomes increasingly entangled with memories of the young woman. An impulsive family holiday to Tenerife becomes an increasingly surreal attempt to escape grief and reconnect with the past.

A favorite in Cannes, where it won Best Film of the Un Certain Regard section, Everytime has been nominated for Best Film and Wollner for Best Screenplay at the 2027 European Film Awards.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with director Sandra Wollner here.

Check out the teaser for the film below.

Industry observers note that yannis Economides crafts a modern Greek tragedy out of the story of a businessman who devises what appears to be a foolproof scheme to save his family home from falling into the hands of a loan shark. But his plan sets a series of increasingly unpredictable events in motion, threatening to destroy the very life he is trying to preserve.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Guatemalan auteur Jayro Bustamante returns with an action-tinged drama inspired by the true story of Guatemala’s 2018 Volcán de Fuego tragedy. María Mercedes Coroy plays a volcanologist who tries to warn and evacuate Indigenous communities as a latest volcano forms amid corruption and economic interests. This is Bustamante’s fourth Oscar submission, after 2015’s Ixcanul, 2019’s La Llorona (shortlisted) and Rita from 2024.

Check out the official trailer (no subtitles) below.

Industry observers note that snow falls on Hong Kong in Juno Mak’s underworld epic, in which a hospital bombing kills a pharmaceutical magnate and leaves his younger son with an unusual ambition for a family drug empire — to shut it all down. A long-in-the-making saga starring Asian industry heavyweights Takeshi Kaneshiro, Tony Leung Ka-fai and Louis Koo, the film premiered in Cannes and won eight Hong Kong Film Awards, including one for its score by the late Ryuichi Sakamoto.

Tony Leung Chiu-wai, Léa Seydoux and fast-rising German star Luna Wedler feature in this century-spanning contemplative drama from Hungarian auteur Ildikó Enyedi (On Body and Soul, The Story of My Wife). Set in three different eras — 1908, 1972, and 2020 — it follows three very different people, a pioneering female student, a lovesick young man and a Hong Kong neuroscientist who share a connection to an ancient ginkgo tree growing int the botanical garden of a German university town. Enigmatic but never self-serious, Silent Friend leavens its massive ideas and visual poetry with a healthy dose of deadpan humor.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with Silent Friend star Luna Wedler here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Industry observers note that yrsa Roca Fannberg turns her camera on the residents and caregivers of a Reykjavík nursing home in this observational documentary about ageing and the final stages of life. Everyday activities, from dancing and exercise classes to painting nails and sharing quiet moments, become the focus of an intimate portrait of a community negotiating the realities of old age. Rather than concentrating on decline, the film finds moments of companionship, humour and pleasure in the routines of institutional life.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

According to recent reports, set in a remote Naga village near the Myanmar border in the early 1960s, Theja Rio’s debut feature follows Anghba, the community’s last surviving chief. With most of the villagers having left, he remains with his ailing wife and speech-impaired son, struggling to preserve the traditions of his ancestors. The arrival of an American missionary introduces Christianity and newly introduced social customs, deepening the generational divide between father and son. The film won the Platform Award at Toronto, qualifying it for the Oscar race.

Read THR India‘s review of Angh here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

In Santosh Davakhar’s Marathi-language folk thriller, a young bride in rural Maharashtra plots her groom’s murder during the traditional ceremony meant to bless their marriage. As the village gathers for the gondhal, an all-night ritual of devotional song and dance, Suman (Ishita Deshmukh) recruits the groom’s cousin, a former suitor, to do the killing so she can run away with one of the performers. The film won Davakhar the Silver Peacock for best director at the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

Director Kamila Andini (Yuni) drew on the testimony of sexual assault survivors for this magical realist drama about the patriarchal structures of a Javanese mountain village. Putri Marino plays Pertiwi, who spent 20 years in prison for killing an accomplice to her rape at 16. She comes home to find the men who sent her away now running the village. When she meets a deaf teenage girl whose ordeal echoes her own, Pertiwi rallies her fellow outcasts to bring the abuse to light. The film premiered in Toronto, and Marino shared the best performance prize at the Singapore International Film Festival.

In a recent development, babak Khajehpasha’s anti-war drama captures the lives and dreams of children and adults in Gaza against the backdrop of an ongoing conflict and crisis with Israel. The film cast child actors of Arab, Iranian, Syrian, and Lebanese backgrounds alongside Iranian performers.

Recent findings suggest that rather than depict violent battlefield scenes, the Iranian filmmaker focused on the all-too human impact of war on children as they learn fear, death and waiting are part of their everyday lives. The film also strikes a note of hope that love and life can be kept alive during horrific war and strife.

It has been revealed that the Iraqi feature, which premiered out of competition in Venice, follows a female Kurdish sniper, Vyan, who returns to Mosul to try and rescue her younger sister. She has survived war by suppressing her emotions. When she learns that her younger sister, missing since the ISIS assault in 2014, may still be alive, she goes all out to rescue her. Mustafa, who was born in Iraqi Kurdistan and fled to Norway as a child, found inspiration for the film from an encounter with a female Peshmerga sniper during the 2014 frontline battles, as female Kurdish fighters countered Islamic State attacks.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

A robbery at a rural credit union ends in tragedy, but Damian McCann’s Irish-language thriller works backwards to reveal how three women became involved in the botched operation. Carrie Crowley, Bríd Brennan and Eva-Jane Gaffney star as the unlikely accomplices at the center of a story involving desperation, criminal ambition and a woman on the verge of a breakdown.

Check out the trailer for Aontas below.

The Israeli film, set in 1987, centers on a 12-year-old boy, Boaz, who while preparing for his bar mitzvah is shocked to witness his father having sex in a swimming pool locker room. The boy’s family life is upturned just as the AIDS epidemic takes hold. But a decade later, the father and his older son attempt to reconcile and accept one another.

Rosenthal’s film, titled Independence in Hebrew, premiered at Sundance and won the top best picture award at Israel’s Ophir Awards, automatically making it the country’s Academy Awards entry.

Check out the trailer for Tell Me Everything below.

Industry observers note that paolo Strippoli’s psychological thriller is one of the rare genre romps among the mostly serious dramas in this season’s international Oscar race. Jasmine Trinca plays a housewife so desperate to have the perfect family she makes a faustian bargain with Valeria Bruni Tedeschi’s chain-smoking stranger, triggering a series of events that, over the course of decades, will bring her family crashing down. Upcoming Line has already snatched up English remake rights to this twisty crowd pleaser.

Read THR‘s review of The Spiral here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

According to recent reports, ryusuke Hamaguchi’s first French feature begins as a workplace drama set in a nursing home outside Paris and blossoms into a love story about two women falling for each other’s minds. Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira) asks her overstretched nurses to employ a more humane system of care for residents living with dementia. Watching a play about life in a psychiatric institution, she recognizes her own convictions in the work of its Japanese director, Mari (Tao Okamoto), who is dying of cancer.

The women connect and talk deep into the night, slipping between French and Japanese, and there’s such pleasure in their exchanges that even Mari’s impromptu whiteboard lecture on capitalism feels like a moment of deep emotional connection. Efira and Okamoto shared the best actress prize at Cannes. After winning the international feature Oscar for Drive My Car in 2022, Hamaguchi is again considered a frontrunner this season.

Read THR‘s interview with All of a Sudden co-stars Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira here.

The film’s official trailer is below.

According to recent reports, sink is a drama about a mother navigating her son’s mental health crisis — still a taboo subject in Jordan — by denying her son’s struggles and opting instead to see his emotional withdrawal and disruptive behavior at school as teenage rebellion. So the mother follows her son about with devotion, hoping her guidance at attention will prove a cure. Duraie’s debut feature, following her acclaimed short films Horizon and Give up the Ghost, had its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival, nd.

Industry observers note that abel is a shepherd living on a collective farm in Kazakhstan whose life in thrown into turmoil in the 1990s when, following the collapse of the Soviet Union, collective farms were dismantled and divided up among corrupt leaders. The aging Abel has a choice: play along for a piece of the action or stand up for what he believes is right.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

Writer-director Vincho Nchogu serves up a mix of comedy and drama in her feature debut. Sarah Karei plays Star, an orphaned and unmarried 38-year-old woman in a rural village who risks losing her home unless she can prove her family lineage and claim her land deed. Along the way she has to deal with hostile neighbors, shady organizations and the promise of potential romance. Winner of the audience award at Tribeca and the Best First Feature prize at the BFI London Film Festival.

Blerta Basholli takes a coming-of-age story into the increasingly volatile atmosphere of late-1990s Kosovo. Thirteen-year-old Dua is navigating the usual uncertainties of adolescence when an incident turns her into a target within her community. Her friendship with the outspoken Maki offers a new perspective on the world around her, even as the escalating conflict threatens to overwhelm their lives.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Sources indicate that bekzat Pirmatov blends psychological horror, folklore and family drama in this supernatural tale about a grieving woman plagued by a recurring nightmare in which an unseen presence appears to strangle her in her sleep. Seeking an explanation, she turns to a traditional healer who discovers ominous markings on the bodies of pregnant women. Their investigation leads to the ancient Kyrgyz legend of Albarsty, a malevolent female spirit associated with pregnancy and childbirth.

According to recent reports, A biographical sports drama from Viesturs Kairišs, who co-wrote Ulya with Kārlis Arnolds Avots, Livia Ulman, and Andris Feldmanis. The Cannes-premiering, black-and-white feature is set in rural Soviet Latvia in 1964, where Uļjana “Ulya” Semjonova’s (Kārlis Arnolds Avots) attracts the attention of basketball scouts due to her exceptional height and strength. She’s pulled from farm life into elite sport in this mise-en-scène-embracing portrait of a Latvian legend.

Read THR‘s interview with director Viesturs Kairišs here.

Check out THR‘s portrait of Ulya star and co-screenwriter Karlis Arnolds Avots here.

Lebanon’s Oscar hopeful is a heist thriller about two sisters who concoct an elaborate plan to break into a bank to steal their own money — the cash frozen by the government during the 2019 Lebanese liquidity crisis — to fund a life-saving operation. Director Rami Kodeih co-wrote the film with his wife Nora Mariana inspired by their own experience at the time, when Mariana needed surgery and their savings were inaccessible. George Clooney and Grant Heslov are executive producers for Smokehouse Pictures.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out a clip from the film below.

According to recent reports, how to Divorce During the War is exactly as it sounds — a high-flying executive Marija (Zygimante Elena Jakstaite) chooses the worst possible moment to inform her struggling filmmaker husband Vytas (Marius Repsys) she wants to split up: just one day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Vilnius-set, soul-searching drama won director Andrius Blaževičius a directing award upon its Sundance premiere.

It has been revealed that this jump scare-heavy psychological horror from debut feature filmmaker Cyrus Neshvad (already an Oscar nominee for 2023 short The Red Suitcase) follows a family in dire straits. With their young son not having much time left, Anne and Greg are ready to sacrifice everything to give him one last chance at salvation. But after crossing an unforgivable moral line, they find themselves trapped in a nightmare where every choice comes with an ever-higher price. Child earned its world premiere at the 2026 Raindance Film Festival.

Check out the official trailer below.

Sources indicate that woo Ming Jin drew on his own childhood as a twin for this coming-of-age drama about two teenage brothers in a Malaysian coastal town. At 15, Ali is the only person who understands his twin brother Amir’s way of communicating. When their father remarries, he packs the boys off to work in a salted-fish factory. But it’s their shared crush on their newly introduced English teacher (Indonesian star Dian Sastrowardoyo) that turns the brothers into rivals. The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival.

In a recent development, żejtune is a visually rich Maltese-language drama from the New York-based Alex Camilleri, led by Michela Farrugia as Mar. When her estranged mother passes away, Mar sees her way out of Malta by selling off her inheritance: three pieces of farmland in the countryside. On her journey to claim her land, she meets Nenu, a spirited 80-year-old singer (Nenu Borg) whose vibrant folk music pulls her into the colourful traditions of the island she’s been so eager to escape. The movie hit the festival circuit with appearances at Gothenburg and Tribeca.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

David Pablos’ drama follows Veneno (Víctor Prieto), a rebellious young drifter who sleeps with truckers at roadside diners. He persuades one of his hook ups, Muñeco (Osvaldo Sánchez) to take him deep into the hyper-masculine world of long-haul trucking. The road movie, produced by Diego Luna, won best film in Venice’s Orizzonti section as well as the Queer Lion.

Read THR‘s review of On The Road here.

According to recent reports, mongolia’s struggle to end more than two centuries of Qing rule takes the shape of an espionage thriller in Tamir Bat-Ulzii’s sweeping historical epic. The actor-director casts himself as Namnansuren, the statesman who joined forces with the Buddhist leader Bogd Khan in 1911. The conspirators seek help from Russia while building a network of spies at home. Made to mark the 115th anniversary of Mongolia’s declaration of independence, the film became one of the country’s biggest local hits this year.

In a recent development, biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić drummed up excitement in Sundance with To Hold a Mountain, a documentary shot in the Montenegrin highlands where a shepherdess and her adopted daughter are haunted by the violent death of her mother and must defend their mountain against its transformation into a NATO military training ground. This tender, windswept feature picked up the Grand Jury Prize in Sundance and the Heart of Sarajevo in the fest’s documentary competition section.

Laïla Marrakchi offers a new spin on the familiarly-bleak tale of migrant labor and exploitation in this social realist drama, inspired by real-life cases of Moroccan women who travel to Spain to work as seasonal fruit-pickers. Her protagonist Hasna (Nisrin Erradi) is a flawed, even unlikable character doing what she needs to survive in a world where oppression and coercion are the norm. Strawberries premiered in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section.

Read THR‘s interview with Laila Marrakchi here.

Industry observers note that abinash Bikram Shah’s debut, the first Nepali feature to screen in Cannes’ Official Selection, won the jury prize in Un Certain Regard. The richly-realized missing-person thriller follows Pirati (Pushpa Thing Lama), the matriarch of a Kinnar community of trans women in rural Nepal. Pirati dreams of slipping away with the man she loves. But when one of the young women she calls her daughters vanishes on a night patrol to keep wild elephants out of the village, she puts those plans on hold to search for her.

Read THR India’s interview with Abinash Bikram Shah here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Afghan-Dutch filmmaker Dawood Hilmandi turns the camera on his own family history in this intimate documentary about war, exile and an attempt at reconciliation with his estranged father. Having fled Afghanistan and later Iran, Hilmandi has made a home in Amsterdam, but a personal loss prompts him to return to his father, an aging, authoritarian former mujahideen fighter. Together they revisit the past, travelling between Iran and Afghanistan in an effort to overcome decades of silence, inherited trauma and estrangement. The film won three prizes at IDFA, including Best First Feature and the FIPRESCI international critics award.

Check out the trailer for Paikar below.

Industry observers note that sisters Ade and Titi lead very different lives under the shadow of their late father. The older Ade (Bimbo Akintola) is a devout Christian and the family’s sole breadwinner, while Titi (Tosin Adeyemi) is an aspiring singer full of independent spirit. When their ailing mother comes to live with them, old resentments resurface, forcing both sisters to confront grief and the fragile bonds that hold a family together.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

In a recent development, kosara Mitić’s debut feature 17, co-written by Ognjen Sviličić, arrived at this year’s Berlinale with a fierce exploration of sexual trauma and female solidarity. The movie follows seventeen-year-old Sara (Eva Kostic), who’s hiding a secret during a school trip. When the trip spirals out of control and she witnesses her friend Lina being sexually assaulted, the two girls try to break the cycle of casual violence and seal an everlasting bond between them in the process.

Read THR‘s interview with 17 director Kosara Mitić here.

Recent findings suggest that hans Petter Moland adapts Knut Hamsun’s Nobel Prize-winning novel about a man determined to make a life in the Norwegian wilderness. Isak arrives in the remote landscape with little more than his willingness to work the land. His relationship with Inger leads to a family and a more permanent settlement, but the couple’s struggle to survive the harsh conditions is gradually complicated by the arrival of the outside world.

Check out the trailer for The Growth of the Soil below.

In August 2023, eight passengers, six of them schoolboys, found themselves dangling in a cable car 900 feet above a ravine in northern Pakistan. Mohammed Ali Naqvi pieced together what followed from cellphone and drone footage, interviews and re-creations, as army commandos and local volunteers raced to save them. The film premiered at Sundance and is the first documentary Pakistan has submitted for the international feature Oscar.

Read THR’s review of Hanging by a Wire here.

Read THR‘s interview with Mohammed Ali Naqvi here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Recent findings suggest that osama is a professional photographer, and upcoming father, living in Gaza who, at the start of the Gaza war, turns to photojournalism to support his wife and infant child. Balancing duty and hope, Ahmed Hassouna’s documentary provides a cinematic portrait of resilience and humanity in wartime. The last two Oscar submission from Palestine: Palestine 36 and From Ground Zero, both made the shortlist but were not nominated.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

The drama, from directors Aarón Bromley and Arturo Montenegro, is set in 1980s against backdrop of Peru’s war between the Shining Path guerrillas and the army. It follows Josué (Junior Bejar), who flees armed conflict in his Peruvian Andes village to migrate to Panama in pursuit of a boxing career and a better future.

Check out the trailer for Chichero below (no subtitles).

Industry observers note that narciso, a charismatic musician with rock ’n’ roll in his veins, returns to Asunción from Buenos Aires and becomes a symbol of freedom after being found dead at the height of his career. This period drama is freely inspired by the 1959 killing of radio host Bernardo Aranda, which led the Paraguay dictatorship to persecute gay men. Written, produced, directed and edited by Marcelo Martinessi, whose The Heiresses was Paraguay’s 2018 Oscar submission, Narciso won the FIPRESCI Prize for best film in Berlin’s Panorama section.

Check out THR Espanol‘s review of Narciso here.

The film’s official trailer (without subtitles) is below.

It has been revealed that paolo Tizón’s visceral observational doc, which premiered at Karlovy Vary, chronicles young military recruits as they as they go through gruelling training in an elite Peruvian military unit battling drug trafficking. The filmmaker spent 10 months embedded with the recruits to capture the hermetic world in his directorial debut.

Check out the trailer for Night Has Come below.

Rafael Manuel turns a sweltering day at an exclusive golf club outside Manila into a deadpan, formalist satire of the Philippine class system. As 17-year-old Isabel (Jorrybell Agoto) tees up balls for the wealthy members, Manuel often frames her face between a golfer’s legs. When she ventures beyond the driving range, even sneaking a taste of a cake the guests have left untouched feels like an act of defiance. Manuel expanded his Berlin Silver Bear-winning short into this debut feature, which won a special jury award for creative vision at Sundance.

Read THR‘s interview with Rafael Manuel here.

Paweł Pawlikowski, an Oscar winner for Ida (2013) and Best Director and Best International Feature nominee for Cold War (2018), returns to European history with this black-and-white drama about German writer Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler) and his journey back to his homeland in 1949 after 16 years in exile. Accompanied by his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller) Mann travels across the country, now divided into a U.S.-supported West and a Soviet-controlled East, confronting the political and personal contradictions of postwar Germany, as well as his own complicated relationship with his homeland.

Read THR‘s review of Fatherland here.

Listen to THR‘s Awards Chatter interview with Fatherland star Sandra Hüller here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Sources indicate that at 80, Arménio is finding it increasingly difficult to live independently and is reluctantly moved into a nursing home. A former soldier who fought in Portugal’s colonial war in Angola, he carries memories and prejudices that have never been fully confronted. António Ferreira’s drama follows his uneasy adjustment to institutional life and his developing friendship with Hermínia, a Black caregiver whose patience and compassion challenge his assumptions about the world and his own past.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

A Romanian couple’s attempt to build a fresh life in Norway becomes the subject of a bitter cultural and ideological confrontation in Cristian Mungiu’s latest drama. Lisbet and Mihai, played by Renate Reinsve and Sebastian Stan, are evangelical Christians whose approach to raising their children attracts the attention of local child-protection authorities. As allegations of abuse threaten to separate the family, the couple find themselves caught between their religious convictions and a state determined to intervene. Mungiu won his second Palme d’Or in Cannes this year with Fjord, and the film is an Oscar frontrunner.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with Fjord director Cristian Mungiu here.

Check out the trailer for Fjord below.

This is a double debut – director Marie Clémentine Dusabejambo’s first feature and Rwanda’s inaugural international Oscar entry. The drama, which explores the long road to justice and reconciliation for survivors of the Rwandan genocide won both the Caméra d’Or for best first feature and the FIPRESCI international critics Prize at Cannes.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR’s interview with Marie Clémentine Dusabejambo here.

Check out a teaser for the film below.

It has been revealed that anas Ba-Tahaf’s black comedy follows the complicated romance between a woman (Sarah Taibah, who also wrote the screenplay), convinced a generational curse will kill her on her 30th birthday, and a heart surgeon who, every operation, has to suppress his urge to kill his patients. Set in contemporary Jeddah, the film premiered at the Red Sea Film Festival last year.

Check out the trailer for ther film below.

In a recent development, this deeply personal documentary from director Mamadou Khouma Gueye (the title, Liti Liti, translates as “The Attachment”), is in the Guinaw-Rails neighborhood in the Senegalese capital of Dakar where the filmmaker grew up. The district is being bulldozed to make way for the Dakar Regional Express Train, leaving residents, such as the director’s mother, displaced. Senegal has only ever submitted six films for the Oscars, but three of them have made the shortlist.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Nenad Pavlović directs a screenplay from Jovan Popović in the arthouse indie Wanderlust. The black-and-white, self-described avant-garde film is based on the 1957 novel Izlet by Serbian painter and film director Mica Popovic. It follows a grieving young artist who flees society to create art in absolute solitude on a deserted island, only to learn that isolation can be as imprisoning as the world he left behind.

Recent findings suggest that koh Jia Ler was a schoolboy when Anthony Chen cast him opposite Yeo Yann Yann in Ilo Ilo, Singapore’s 2013 Oscar submission. In the final film of the trilogy Chen continued with Wet Season (2019), Koh plays a young man whose girlfriend is pregnant. His widowed father, a noodle seller, has fallen for a beer waitress played by Yeo. Chen’s portrait of two generations trying to build a family became the first Singaporean film selected for the Berlin International Film Festival’s main competition, where it received strong reviews.

THR‘s review of We Are All Strangers.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Production organization Silverart describes Martin Gonda’s feature debut as the highest-rated Slovak film of 2025. Inspired by true events — the displacement of the Rusyn people over the construction of the Starina reservoir — it is set in 1980 communist Czechoslovakia, where Mara (Sára Chripáková) dreams of leaving her village to study and become a pilot. But her father, a Rusyn farmer and widower, insists she stays and works the land. As the construction of the reservoir looms, Gonda depicts the struggle between tradition, identity, and the desire for freedom.

Check out the official trailer below.

In a recent development, earning its world premiere at Locarno, Fantasy is from the mononymous Slovenian-Macedonian filmmaker Kukla (full name Katarina Rešek) in her feature film debut. Gender, desire and self-discovery come to the forefront in this tale of three best friends living in a fictional Slovenian industrial town. A chance encounter with Fantasy (Alina Juhart), a young transgender woman, might just change their lives for the better.

Read THR‘s interview with director Kukla here.

Check out the official trailer below.

According to recent reports, winner of the Tiger Award at this year’s Rotterdam Film Festival, this drama from co-directors Devon Delmar and Jason Jacobs tells the story of an 80-year-old Namaqualand goat herder who is in danger of losing her independence after she falls victim to a scam promising reparation for her father’s unpaid service during World War II. Jacobs cast his own grandmother to play the lead.

Read THR‘s interview with Delmar here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Eight years after Burning became the first South Korean film shortlisted for the international feature Oscar, Korean maestro Lee Chang-dong returned to Venice with a characteristically searing drama about what capitalism is doing to human dignity — and whether art has any power to critique the system that bankrolls it. Sul Kyung-gu plays an autoworker shattered by the violent end to a strike at his factory. His wife (Jeon Do-yeon) befriends a documentary filmmaker (Cho Yeo-jeong) whose tycoon husband (Zo In-sung) patiently supports her interest in workers’ rights.

Both a powerful love story and a meta-fictional exploration of the ethics of filmmaking, much of the film’s drama explores the slippery line between the artist’s sympathy for her subjects and the desire for a good scene. The Netflix film won Venice’s Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize. Jeon, who previously became the first Korean to win best actress at Cannes for Lee’s Secret Sunshine, is now considered a strong contender in the lead actress Oscar race.

Read THR‘s review of Possible Love.

Read THR‘s interview with Lee Chang-dong.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

In a recent development, the sweeping gay historical epic La Bola Negra won Los Javis the coveted Best Director prize in Cannes this year, immediately entering the international — and domestic — awards conversation. Weaving together three interconnected storylines from 1932, 1937, and 2017, the critic darling puts queer desire, repression and Spain’s inherited stories up on the major screen, hurling breakout stars Guitarricadelafuente and Miguel Bernardeau into the mainstream and potentially giving The Odyssey a run for its Best Picture money.

Read THR‘s behind-the-scenes deep dive into the making of the film here.

Check out THR‘s portrait of La Bola Negra breakout star Guitarricadelafuente here.

The film’s official trailer is below.

Three police officers escort a prisoner across Sri Lanka’s Knuckles mountains toward the village where he grew up. The officers have reason to expect he won’t make it home alive. But it’s a long drive, and their captive proves an unexpectedly agreeable traveling companion. Lalith Rathnayake’s second feature won prizes for screenplay and cinematography in the Asian New Talent competition at the Shanghai International Film Festival.Official trailer below.

In a recent development, an ordinary family is crushed by economic forces beyond their control in director Visar Morina’s social drama, which won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize in Sundance, qualifying it for Oscar consideration. Husband and wife Hatixhe and Shaban work a small dairy farm in rural Kosovo to support their three daughters and extended family. But when a family dispute costs them their livelihood, they are forced to move to the capital Pristina in search of work, only to find themselves struggling with low wages and the high cost of housing.

Read THR‘s review of Shame and Money here.

Read THR‘s interview with director Visar Morina here.

It has been revealed that podcaster and journalist Alex Schulman makes his feature film debut with Adult Supervision, a black comedy that allowed him to work with his once-public enemy Gustav Skarsgård. The second-born son of the Swedish family dynasty stars as anxiety-ridden Bill, who accompanies his daughter and her school friends on a remote trip, desperate to repair their icy relationship. He has help from two fellow fathers: the secretly domineering Bobo (Fares Fares) and Pontus (Linus Wahlgren), but tensions quickly escalate, and their grip on the situation begins to slip.

Read THR‘s interview with Alex Schulman here.

Check out the official trailer below.

Nicolas Wadimoff has long dominated the doc and feature film space with his politically provocative work, and continues that trend with the harrowing, Venice-premiering documentary Who Is Still Alive. Described by the filmmaker as “an absolute necessity,” the project spotlights nine voices from Gaza. The group — made up of women and men, old and young — reflects on life before and during the ongoing war with Israel, outlining their neighborhoods in chalk from memory and detailing their close relationships with the friends, neighbors and family they’ve now lost.

Read THR’s interview with Nicolas Wadimoff here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

In a recent development, shortly after Bashar al-Assad fell in December 2024, filmmaker Tawfik Sabouni returned to Saidnaya, the prison outside Damascus known as “the other side of the sun.” A former inmate, Sabouni invited four fellow survivors back into the cells to reconstruct for his camera the brutal rituals by which they had lived. The documentary premiered in Berlin’s Panorama section and won both the critics’ and audience prizes at the Amman International Film Festival.

Check out the trailer for The Other Side of the Sun below.

Sources indicate that in 1954, during Taiwan’s White Terror, a teenager travels alone from Chiayi to Taipei to buy back the body of her executed brother. She nearly falls into the hands of traffickers before a discharged soldier takes up her cause. Written and directed by Chen Yu-hsun (My Missing Valentine), the film won four Golden Horse Awards, including best narrative feature and original screenplay.

Check out the trailer for A Foggy Tale below.

Sompot Chidgasornpongse drew on the Buddhist pilgrimages of his childhood for this gently comic family road movie. When a fortune teller warns that his elderly mother may soon die, Sakol packs three generations into a van to visit nine temples in a single day. Nine is an auspicious number in Thailand, and Sakol hopes the family’s offerings to the monks will earn enough merit to prolong his mother’s life. A few stops in, Mom is too tired to get out of the van.

Produced by Chidgasornpongse’s longtime collaborator Apichatpong Weerasethakul, his fiction feature debut premiered in Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight and won directing and acting prizes in Shanghai’s Asian Upcoming Talent competition.

Check out the trailer to 9 Temples to Heaven below.

A retired civil engineer gives his Syrian caregiver money to take her two young sons to Europe. Instead, she leaves the boys with him and disappears, just as his grown children arrive for Eid al-Adha with claims of their own on the family’s resources. Tunç Davut’s family drama premiered at Turkey’s Antalya Film Festival.

Check out the trailer for Like a Limbless Tree below.

Trauma, resistance and hope loom large over Alisa Kovalenko’s Traces, which picked up the Berlinale’s audience award this year. The documentary follows the stories of six Ukrainian women — from Donbas to the Kherson region and the Kyiv area — who survived conflict-related sexual violence and torture during Russia’s aggression and refuse to remain silent.

The film’s official trailer is below.

Industry observers note that former child star and documentarian Pegah Ahangarani charts over 40 years of turbulent political history in Iran with Rehearsals for a Revolution, crafted entirely around her own family archives. The final product, which won Ahangarani Cannes’ Golden Eye award for best documentary, is a portrait of a country shaped by political repression and in constant hope for radical change.

Recent findings suggest that “I realized, ‘Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools,’” Ahangarani told THR about drawing inspiration from her relatives’ photos, videos and voice recordings. “Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship [and] the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe.”.

THR‘s review of Rehearsals for a Revolution.

Read THR‘s interview with Pegah Ahangarani here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your current morning ritual involves violently hitting refresh on a dozen retail tabs, you already know the vibe: finding the Nintendo Switch 2: The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition is turning into an Olympic sport.

We're closely monitoring inventory at all the major retailers and are cautiously optimistic it will be restocked for the holiday shopping season. On the question of if/when the limited-edition Zelda Switch 2 will be restocked, a Nintendo spokesperson provided this not-entirely-reassuring statement to Mashable: "Although we cannot provide detailed information, we are striving to ensure that we can supply our products to those who want them.".

Between automated bot armies scooping digital drops, surprise order cancellations at Walmart, and inventory vanishing in seconds on Amazon, this custom black-and-gold console feels like a myth. But while digital storefronts look completely barren, stock is actively circulating behind the scenes.

Before getting into the restock details, bookmark these retailer pages to check for surprise drops:.

Nintendo Store — Out of stock right now, but you can add it to your wishlist to get pinged the second a restock hits.

Amazon — Dropping tiny batches of consoles randomly throughout the day.

Walmart — Stock exists but only for third-party listings selling at way over market price, so make sure your in-stock email alerts are turned on.

Target — Sold out online, but periodic drops have taken place in-store.

Best Buy — Sold out online, but select stores ran midnight openings on Nov. 5 with walk-in stock.

GameStop — Online orders are off; you will have to walk into a store to find one.

The feeding frenzy is being supercharged by Nintendo’s staggered release calendar. While the custom Zelda 40th Anniversary hardware dropped first on Oct. 29, the flagship game driving demand — The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 — arrived on Thursday, Nov. 5.

The remake rebuilds the 1998 classic from the ground up with modernized controls, a fully orchestrated soundtrack, reworked dungeon puzzles, and expanded Hyrule environments. Since the $520 console doesn’t include the game, everyone is rushing to lock down a system before launch day.

Industry observers note that the package includes the special-edition Switch 2 system sporting a custom black-and-gold finish, themed Joy-Con 2 controllers, and a matching dock decorated with the gold Triforce emblem. It retains the platform's signature flexibility, letting you switch between TV, Tabletop, and Handheld modes whenever you want. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Inside the themed chassis, you get 256GB of built-in storage (expandable with microSD Express cards), a vivid display in handheld mode, faster load times, and support for up to 4K resolution on compatible TVs when the console sits in the dock.

The magnetic Joy-Con 2 controllers add mouse-style tracking in supported games, while the fresh GameChat hub lets you voice chat and share your screen directly as you play. It also plays your older Switch games and supports standard multiplayer options.

Landing limited-edition Nintendo hardware takes a little prep work, but these battle-tested habits will give you a real edge over the bots:.

Hands off the refresh button in Best Buy's queue — When an online drop goes live, Best Buy puts shoppers into a randomized waiting line to filter out scrapers. Touching the reload button resets your spot and boots you straight to the back.

Watch for Walmart+ early-access paywalls — Walmart frequently locks headline console drops behind paid Walmart+ subscriptions for the first 30 to 60 minutes. If you have a membership, keep that tab signed in; if not, wait for the general public window to unlock.

According to recent reports, dodge third-party sellers — Double-check the seller before buying. Marketplace scalpers frequently list units for jacked-up prices; make sure it says "Sold and shipped by [Retailer]" at the standard price.

Skip the web wars and head to physical stores — Online checkout bots grab website stock in under 15 seconds. Showing up in person is easily your most reliable path to securing one without paying scalper markups.

Hopefully, yes, but this hasn't been confirmed.

Stores like Walmart, Amazon, and Best Buy often hold onto popular gaming hardware to use as headline deals during Black Friday and Cyber Monday week.

According to recent reports, with that said, Black Friday restocks are usually the hardest ones to catch. You will be fighting website crashes, gift shoppers, and automated bots all at once. If you can grab a console whenever stock appears, take it. Think of Black Friday as a backup proposal, not your main bet.

Console hunting sucks right now, period. But between the surprise micro-drops and physical store restocks, you still have real shots at retail price — just be ready to move the second that stock goes live.

#196548. Navigating grief in academia: ways to find balance

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1312 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Navigating grief in academia: ways to find balance

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1312 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pamela Yeh with her mother in Los Angeles, California, in the late 1970s.Credit: Courtesy of Pamela Yeh.
  • In a recent development, there are few things in this world that are more universal than grief.
  • My mother grew up in deep poverty in Taiwan and she worked relentlessly throughout her life to give me and my siblings many opportunities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pamela Yeh with her mother in Los Angeles, California, in the late 1970s.Credit: Courtesy of Pamela Yeh.

In a recent development, there are few things in this world that are more universal than grief. And yet, each person’s own particular grief can feel as unique as the person they are grieving for. I have been in academia for decades, but have heard little about grief in that time, so I wanted to share a few tips that helped me get through the early stages of grief when my mother died last year.

My mother grew up in deep poverty in Taiwan and she worked relentlessly throughout her life to give me and my siblings many opportunities. She was the first in her family to go to college, and at 23 years old, she moved to Canada to work as a nurse. After a few years of enduring Canadian winters, she had had enough and moved to sunny California. She met my dad there, and a few years later she gave birth to my sister, then me and then my brother. She raised us while working several jobs as a nurse. She cheered the three of us on throughout our lives. That’s not to say that she ever fully understood my career: she once described my work (I am an evolutionary biologist, specializing in birds and bacteria, at the University of California, Los Angeles) as “counting birds”.

She was adventurous, but between her family and work responsibilities, she didn’t have much time to travel. So, once she retired, I took her on fieldwork and conference trips with me whenever I could — to China, the Netherlands, Italy, Mexico, Japan and throughout the United States.

It has been revealed that when her grandchildren came along, she helped them to learn how to read, to do maths and to speak Chinese. In the last years of her life, I had a small house built for her in our back garden in Los Angeles, so she would always be close to me. When you lose someone who is extremely close to you, your world is never the same.

When a loved one dies: how academia can support bereaved colleagues.

When a loved one dies: how academia can support bereaved colleagues.

In a recent development, in the weeks and months after she died, I found myself in a fog of shock and grief. I felt the need to be moving constantly: running, walking the dog, cleaning the house. At times, I could not be certain of my ability to conduct the high-level abstract and conceptual thinking that academia often requires, so I turned to Trevor Price, my former PhD adviser at the University of California, San Diego (who is now at the University of Chicago, Illinois). I explained my brain fog and deep grief, and he read over my work and made sure that I didn’t miss any crucial scientific arguments in some of the papers I was writing. Although I graduated more than two decades ago, he did not hesitate for one second to help me.

People won’t know that you need help until you reach out. And the earlier you do it, the more time and energy you can give yourself and the easier it will be for others to help.

Here are some tips that helped me to navigate the academic world while grieving.

Recent findings suggest that ideally, you should determine what support is available before it is needed. Institutions often have all sorts of resources and benefits for people experiencing grief. These might include time off for a bereavement, leave for family care, counselling and a break from teaching classes. I never knew, until my mother passed away, that I could have taken paid leave to take care of her while she was unwell: she had a debilitating stroke five months before she died. Make sure you understand (and ask questions) about your work contract and what your employer offers.

Sometimes, a family member’s illness can occur suddenly, and other times it might start off as one condition and snowball into something else. Talk to the chair of your department and to your colleagues as early as possible about getting cover for your courses and committees. Be creative and brainstorm which other people — including your colleagues, former advisers and former students and postdocs — might be able to step in and give your conference talks, guest lecture for your classes and conduct other activities that you might need help with.

Pamela Yeh (centre) with her parents, husband, son and dog on the front steps of her home in Los Angeles, California, in 2014.Credit: Courtesy of Pamela Yeh.

Sources indicate that I learnt this the hard way. I did not reach out to people early enough and was unrealistically optimistic about my mother’s health trajectory. While I waited for her to get better, I was so panicked about the thought of losing her that I became incapacitated. I couldn’t focus and, at times, I could barely do simple tasks such as answering e-mails, or making appointments for meetings. I told myself as soon as she was better, which would be any day now, I would catch up. And so, I didn’t have a realistic plan in place when she died.

Industry observers note that you have to accept that you might not be at your best when it comes to research productivity, mentoring and teaching while you’re grieving. Ask someone to help with advising your students, and rely on colleagues or former students. You might have to reduce the frequency with which you meet your students, hold laboratory meetings and work with collaborators, and resort to advising through e-mail and video calls. And you might have to give less detailed comments on your students’ writing. I did all of the above during the first few weeks and months of grieving. I had an especially hard time giving advice to my graduate students who were doing field work. Ellie Diamant, a former PhD student of mine who is now a biologist at Bard College in Annandale-On-Hudson, Latest York, generously stepped in and met with many of my students. It took me a while to understand and accept that I simply wasn’t going to meet the normal standards I set for myself while going through this difficult time.

Industry News: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space.
  • Newly introduced research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes.
  • In a recent development, the discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

Newly introduced research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

In a recent development, the discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

A Hidden Population of Black Holes.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," states LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

In a recent development, chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

Despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses.

To investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

According to recent reports, even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

Industry observers note that "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred states. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

Sources indicate that the researchers also examined how swiftly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths.

It has been revealed that finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

Recent findings suggest that "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred states. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

It has been revealed that by studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The upcoming findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

The research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.
